sections.title: Why relational data is different
blocks: Pretrained transformers changed language and vision: one general architecture, trained on a lot of data, transfers to new tasks with little or no extra training. Relational data has no such model yet, although relational databases are the dominant store of structured enterprise information . The difficulty is the shape of the data. A database is several tables with columns of mixed types, and rows are linked across tables by primary and foreign keys. The signal for a prediction is scattered across rows, columns, linked tables and time .

Take the question this course follows. Will Anna Müller (customer 35), a customer of the synthetic shop ShopDB, place no order in the 30 days after 2025-03-01? The customer’s own row in customers holds a name, a country, an age, a premium flag and a signup date. The evidence is in other tables: the 31 orders placed before that date, the products those orders point to, the reviews written, and whether the customer went quiet in earlier months. A model has to gather that evidence across keys and respect time: to predict at a time t, it may only use rows created before t .
There are four established ways to hand such a database to a model. Each keeps something and loses something.
Four ways to hand ShopDB to a model
Every view is built from the live ShopDB around the running example. Switch tabs to compare; none of these is how RT reads the data.

The paper’s verdict is that none of these provides a viable backbone for a foundation model on relational databases . RT is designed around three principles instead: capture the relational structure while keeping the natural symmetries of relational data, support flexible self-supervised pretraining, and generalize zero-shot across heterogeneous schemas .

In one sentence: RT reads a context window of cells sampled around a seed row, and predicts the one masked cell of that row . The prediction is either a logit, for a yes/no target like churn, or a z-score, for a number . The model itself is short: once the masks are built, the path from cells to the final vectors is the 22 lines below.

sections.title: Three ideas
blocks: The paper names three innovations . Each one below comes with the live example.
1. Cells are tokens

RT “represents each database cell as a token, with embeddings constructed from its value, column name and table name” . A cell token is a triple (v, c, t): value, column, table . The value goes through a small encoder for its type: number, text, datetime or boolean. The column and table enter together as the text embedding of the phrase “<column> of <table>”, made by a frozen sentence encoder . Key columns produce no tokens, only links, and missing values produce nothing .
What becomes of every cell of the seed row and its parent row
Keys turn into links, missing values disappear, and every other cell becomes one token labeled with its phrase.

Why cells and not rows? A cell is the unit every database shares, whatever its schema. And once cells are tokens, any prediction task becomes “fill in this masked cell”, the same objective RT is pretrained on .
2. The task is a table

A forecasting task such as churn has no column in the database: its labels must be computed from future rows . RT stores them in a task table, one row per entity and timestamp, holding a foreign key to the entity, the timestamp and the label . With task-table prompting, that table is attached to the database. Only one task table is active at a time, its rows serve as seed rows, and to the model it is an ordinary table .

The payoff is in what the sampler finds next to the seed. The same entity’s earlier task rows are its children, so they enter the context like any other row, with their labels visible : in-context labels. The paper stresses that this is not few-shot learning, since no explicit subgraph-label pairs are required . In the live context, 12 earlier churn labels of Anna are visible.
Every customer-churn row of customer 35, on a time line
Rows dated after the seed never reach its context . Hover a marker for its split and label.
3. Structure lives in the attention masks

The database’s structure is not written into the tokens. It enters through relational attention: each block runs four attention layers with the same arithmetic and different masks. Column attention connects cells of the same column, feature attention connects a cell to its own row and the rows it points to, neighbor attention connects it to the rows that point to its row, and full attention connects everything . There are no positional encodings, so the order of tables, rows and columns does not matter .
Who the masked cell may attend to, in each layer
One strip per mask, one mark per token of the live context, in sequence order; colored marks are the allowed keys. Hover a strip to name a token.

On this context the masked cell sees 13 tokens through column attention, 7 tokens through feature attention, none through neighbor attention and all 128 through full attention. Information from elsewhere still arrives, over several steps: the customer’s cells read the orders that point to them in a neighbor layer, and the masked cell reads the customer’s cells in the next block’s feature layer. That reading follows from the masks; it is not a claim of the paper . Chapters 9 to 11 follow those paths.

Each sublayer is a residual update of the normalized stream (pre-norm), in the order column, feature, neighbor, full . The paper’s Algorithm 2 writes the norm after the attention instead; the code is what ran .

sections.title: What zero-shot means here
blocks: The paper defines zero-shot relational learning as “predicting new targets on a new RDB with a new schema, without weight updates. Information about the new RDB is available only at inference time, solely through the context window” . To test it, the authors pretrain separately for each target database on all tasks of all the other databases, a leave-one-database-out protocol . This site runs one such split: it pretrains on SchoolDB, RacingDB and ForumDB and holds out ShopDB.
Leave one database out, on this site

At test time nothing is retrained. For each seed row of the new database the sampler builds a context, one forward pass runs with frozen weights, and the output at the masked cell is the prediction . Whatever the model learns about ShopDB, it learns from that window: the cell values, the column and table names as text, which cells share a column, a row or a link, and the past labels of the task that happen to be in it .
Ask the frozen model about another seed row
Each pick samples that row’s context and runs one forward pass with the same weights. It does not change the rest of the course unless you press the button.

sections.title: Tables, rows, columns, cells
blocks: A relational database is a collection of tables linked through relationships between them. Each table is made of rows, and every row is a set of cells, one for each column . That small vocabulary is all RT needs, and it takes it literally: one cell becomes one token .

Our running database is ShopDB, a synthetic online shop with 4 tables: 80 customers, 30 products, 1,286 orders and 303 reviews, recorded from 2024-01-07 to 2025-06-30. It plays the part of a database the model has never seen: the miniature RT on this site was pretrained on three other synthetic databases, and ShopDB was held out (chapter 13).
Anatomy of a table: a few orders rows
Pick a word to see what it refers to. The rows are real rows of the live database.

sections.title: The ShopDB schema
blocks: A database’s schema lists its tables with their columns and data types, together with the relational structure . In the diagram below each card is a table. A key icon marks the primary key and a link icon a foreign key, with an arrow to the table it references. Every other column is a feature column, drawn with its type glyph: # for numbers, Aa for text, a clock for datetimes and a toggle for booleans. The time column is one of the feature columns; it also carries a time tag.
ShopDB: tables, keys and links
Hover a table to trace its links; click or tap it to open it in the table browser below.

The shape is worth a second look. customers and products have no foreign keys: nothing points out of them. orders (→ customers, products) and reviews (→ customers, products) hold foreign keys, and each also has a time column. Events point to the entities they involve.

Schemas differ from one database to the next. That is why the paper argues that pretraining needs a schema-agnostic architecture, one that takes in the multi-table structure through attention masks . RT never receives this diagram as such. It sees cells, each labeled with its column and table name, plus the links between rows (chapters 4, 5 and 9).
how a table declares its keys and time column

Each table file carries three metadata entries: pkey_col, fkey_col_to_pkey_table and time_col. They tell preprocessing which column is the primary key, which columns are foreign keys and to which table, and which column is the time column .

Table browser
The number on the left of each row is its position, and it equals the primary key: customers[35] has customer_id = 35. RT relies on that convention, as the next section shows.

ShopDB has a few gaps on purpose: age is missing for 10 of 80 customers and review_text is missing for 23 of 303 reviews. RT neither imputes nor masks a missing value. The cell simply produces no token, so that row has one token fewer .

sections.title: Keys link rows: F→P and P→F
blocks: Every table has a primary key, and some include foreign keys that reference primary keys in other tables. This induces a graph structure. Connections from foreign keys to primary keys are F→P links, and the reverse incoming connections are P→F links . (The paper’s “every table” is a simplification: the task tables of chapter 3 have no primary key, and the code accepts any table without one . A row is identified by its position anyway .)

In ShopDB, an order’s customer_id and product_id are foreign keys. Each order therefore has two F→P links, up to its customer and its product. Seen from the other end, each customer and each product has P→F links down to its orders and reviews. The row a foreign key points to is the parent; the rows pointing to a row are its children .
Link explorer
Parents sit above the focus row and children below; the graph draws the same rows, with arrows from child to parent (F→P) . A row has few parents, but it can have many children.

Walk around for a moment and an asymmetry shows up. A row has at most one parent per foreign-key column, so no ShopDB row has more than 2. Children are another story: products[4] (27-inch Monitor) is referenced by 313 orders and 67 reviews. The number of F→P links is limited by the number of foreign-key columns, while P→F links have unbounded degree .
Parents per row, at most
one per foreign-key column (orders, reviews)
Children per row, at most
products[4], no limit in principle

A limit of the code, not of the data: each token stores at most 5 parent indices (f2p_nbr_idxs) for the attention masks, and a row with more non-null foreign keys would trip an assertion when its cells are emitted . ShopDB rows need at most 2.

The paper turns this asymmetry into its sampling rule. RT never reads a whole database at once. For each prediction it starts from one row, the seed row, and collects the cells of nearby rows into a context window by walking the key links outward . We call the part of RT that does this walk the sampler (chapter 6). Parent rows typically contain important features (an order links to its customer and its product) and there are few of them, so the sampler follows every F→P link immediately, without subsampling. Informative signals from P→F links often arise through aggregation, with diminishing returns from including many children, so it follows at most w children from any row, the width bound .
The dashed line marks the width bound w: when RT builds a context, it follows at most w children of a row (chapter 6). The bars count every child ever written, before any time filter.

Lines 439-442: the primary-key column is skipped, so it makes no token and no edge. For a foreign key, a null value is skipped (462-464), the parent is ptable_offset + val (477), and its index is pushed onto the row’s parent list f2p_nbr_idxs (479). The continue at the end of the branch (line 532, below this excerpt) means no cell is ever made from a key .
one foreign-key value, two edges
The F→P edge is stored on the child; the P→F edge is appended to the parent’s adjacency list and carries the child’s table and timestamp, which the sampler reads later .

sections.title: Feature columns and key columns
blocks: Now the consequence that matters most for the model. RT does not tokenize rows; it tokenizes cells, and only some of them. Once a row is selected, “all its non-missing feature cells (i.e., cells not from primary- or foreign-key columns)” enter the context . Chapter 6 adds two small exceptions, for a context that fills up and for the leakage columns of autocomplete tasks .
A feature column holds information about the row. A key column (the paper says ID column) only says which row is which and which rows are linked.
What RT keeps of a row
Split the row and watch where each cell goes. Try a row with a missing value from the menu.

The paper is candid about the price of this choice . RT does not incorporate the names of primary-key and foreign-key columns, which often carry useful semantics. And it does not tell apart two foreign keys that point to the same table. The paper’s example is a product table with both buyer_id and seller_id referencing a user table: the model cannot distinguish which user bought and which sold.
Two foreign keys into the same table

No token carries a foreign-key column name. A column name reaches the model only through a cell’s column-name embedding , and key columns make no cells. What remains is the parent list and the edges . ShopDB never has this problem: no table has two foreign keys into the same table.
how preprocessing splits a row

The primary-key column is skipped outright . A foreign-key column produces no token either; each non-null value becomes an entry in the row’s parent list plus a pair of edges . Every remaining column is a feature column. Each of its cells that is neither null nor a NaN float becomes a cell record , whose type follows its storage type . Chapter 4 follows those records into numbers.

UInt32, Int32, Int64 and Float32 values are cast to Float64 and become numbers. A null matches the empty arm on line 552 and leaves no trace. The boolean arm shown here is one of four (number, datetime and text follow in lines 565-605) .

sections.title: Time
blocks: Many relational databases are temporal: timestamp columns record when rows are created . A table may declare one time column. In ShopDB, orders have order_time and reviews have review_time. customers and products have none. Note that customers does have a datetime column, signup_date, but it is an ordinary feature, not the table’s time column.
The time column is still a feature column: order_time becomes a datetime token like any other . It has a second job, though: it gives the row a timestamp that the sampler uses.

Why time matters: “if we want to predict whether a user will buy an item at time t, the model must only use information available before t, otherwise it risks temporal leakage” . Below are all time-stamped rows linked to customers[35] (Anna Müller). The accent line is the prediction time t, set to the simulation seed’s timestamp, 2025-03-01. Everything to its right is the future.
Activity of customers[35] over time
Each mark is one row. Drag on the chart or use the slider to move t; hover a mark for details, click it to make it the focus row.

Inside RT the principle lives in the sampler, and it is narrower. When the sampler visits a row, it first drops the children that are later than the seed. Then it keeps at most w of the database children that remain, chosen uniformly at random (all of them if there are w or fewer) . Parents are never checked. Chapter 6 runs the whole algorithm step by step.
which rows carry a timestamp

The code takes a row’s timestamp from its time column, in whole seconds, but it sets it only inside the loop over foreign keys . A row therefore gets a timestamp only if its table has a time column, its time value is not null, and it has at least one non-null foreign key . Counted in the live preprocessed graph:

A time column alone is therefore not enough. RacingDB, one of the other databases on this site, shows the edge case: its races table declares race_date as its time column but has no foreign key, so none of its 36 rows gets a timestamp in the preprocessed graph .
Nanoseconds divided by 10⁹: whole seconds. Because this runs only for non-null foreign-key values, a table without foreign keys (customers, products) never gets a timestamp, time column or not .
Lines 406-408 push every parent with no time test. Lines 421-424 drop a child only when both timestamps exist and the child’s is later than the seed’s .

sections.title: The database as a graph
blocks: Put all the links together and the database becomes a graph. Relational deep learning (RDL) makes this explicit: it represents a database as a relational entity graph, “a temporal, heterogeneous graph where each table is a node-type, each row an individual node, and every primary-foreign key relationship an edge” . The first models applied graph neural networks directly to that graph; later work refined their message passing and moved to transformer-based architectures .
The neighborhood of customers[35] as an entity graph
Each node is one row, colored and shaped by its table; each arrow is one foreign-key link, child to parent. The dashed rings mark the hop distance from the center row. Click a node to recenter.

The paper’s criticism of these architectures is that they are schema-specific, which prevents pretraining and fine-tuning on diverse database structures . RT keeps the links but changes the unit. When the paper contrasts RT with another relational foundation model, one that first aggregates each table and then runs a graph neural network between tables, it describes its own design this way: “our model uses a cell-level representation of the entire database and employs attention masks to directly represent the foreign-key structure” .
Same rows, two representations

Switch to the cell view: each row breaks into its feature cells, the key cells vanish as tokens, and the links remain as structure. This is not yet a context window; chapter 6 decides which rows enter one.

That is the raw material RT works with: a pool of cells, each knowing its value, its column and its table, plus the links between rows. The next chapter adds the last ingredient, the prediction task. A forecasting task arrives as one more table attached to the database; an autocomplete task just masks a cell of an existing row .

sections.title: Every task is “fill in the masked cell”
blocks: RT has a single job: predict the value of a masked cell. The paper calls this masked token prediction: “predict the value of a masked cell in the database, conditioned on the rest of the observed database” . Two broad families of tasks on relational data fit this mould :
Autocomplete: the missing value belongs to a column that already exists, such as the star rating of a review.
Forecasting: the value is about the future, such as whether a customer will order again. Such targets “do not exist in the original database and must be constructed from future rows” .
Two ways a cell can be missing

Live ShopDB rows. Left: the rating of review 151 is hidden, and the leakage column that would reveal it is dropped. Right: customer 35’s churn label is stored in no ShopDB table; it is computed from the orders after t.

Either way, each training or evaluation example masks exactly one cell: the target cell of its seed row. Every other cell that enters the context stays visible ; autocomplete tasks first drop their leakage columns, as section 4 shows . The type of that cell decides the loss: a boolean target is trained as binary classification, a numeric one as regression .

sections.title: Building customer-churn, step by step

ShopDB’s version is customer-churn: will the customer place no order in the next 30 days? Each row has three columns: a timestamp t, a foreign key customer_id, and the label churn. Like RelBench task tables, it has no primary key . The label summarizes the future window (t, t + Δ], here with Δ = 30 days .

sections.title: Three splits, one table
blocks: RelBench gives every forecasting task three splits : Train rows at the training timestamps, Val rows at the validation cutoff (2025-03-01) and Test rows at the test cutoff (2025-04-15). Each split is a separate file , and RT gives each its own block of node indices . The Test rows keep their labels on disk, as in RelBench’s cached files: the sampler masks only the seed’s own target cell, and evaluation reads the true label from the batch .

Choose where a seed row sits. The sampler skips a task row only if its timestamp is later than the seed’s, so rows at the same timestamp pass . The figure shows only this time filter: whether a row that passes it actually lands in the context depends on the search and on L (chapter 6).

Move the seed to Test: the Val rows are now earlier than the seed, so they pass the filter too, and a Test prediction can use Val labels as context. The time filter skips only rows that lie in the seed’s future .

To RT, the three splits are one logical table. Its name is the task’s directory name and the split only sets the table type . Names are interned once, so all three splits share one table name index and one index per column . Live from the preprocessed ShopDB:

This is why the past matters. Past rows of the same task, from any split, look to the model like ordinary rows of the same table. The sampler reaches them through the customer, and their label cells stay unmasked. They are the in-context labels : “while task rows provide ‘in-context labels’, our setting is not few-shot as explicit subgraph-label pairs are not required” .

In your live context (customer-churn, L = 128, w = 16 scaled down) the seed is customer #35 Anna Müller’s Val row. The seed’s own customer contributes 12 visible past labels, and other customers contribute 0. The search did reach 3 other customers, but only far from the seed (5 hops), and the 128 slots filled up with closer rows before their task rows were taken . Chapter 6 shows the order in which the search takes rows.

Compare the paper’s counts on RelBench, as mean ± sd per 1024-cell context (target entity / other entities): rel-f1 driver-dnf 19 ± 14 / 0 ± 0, and rel-amazon user-churn 4 ± 4 / 1 ± 5 . Those counts predate a sampler change that keeps same-timestamp task rows , which the next note is about.

One more difference concerns time. The paper says it uses “database rows only up to the training cutoff timestamps” , but the paper-era code drops no database row by date; the sampler’s filter on child rows is the only time guard . ShopDB keeps every row, as the code does (chapter 13 has the details).
In the official code
pq_path is tasks/<task>/<split>.parquet: every split gets the same table_name and a different TableType.

sections.title: Regression targets and autocomplete
blocks: A regression task: product-sales

Forecasting labels need not be booleans. product-sales asks how many units of a product will be ordered in (t, t + 30 d]. The recipe is the same as for churn, with a different aggregation: add up the quantities of the window’s orders instead of checking that there are none. The label is a number, so this is regression: a Number target trained with a Huber loss on its z-score . The z-score uses the Train split’s statistics, also for Val and Test rows .
Hover, tap or focus a bar to see the orders it sums; a click pins it, and arrow keys move between windows. Pick any product: this choice stays in this chapter.

In the official code, the loss is picked by the type of the target cell, not by a list of task names . Only evaluation uses a list of task names: it decides which decoder’s output is read and whether the metric is AUROC or R² . RelBench stores some binary labels as 0/1 integers, so preprocessing casts them to booleans, task by task .
In the official code
Each tuple is (database, table, target column, leakage columns). For forecasting, the table is the task table and the leakage list is empty.
Autocomplete: the target is an existing column

Autocomplete needs no new table: “sampling starts from the masked database row” . The seed is a database row and the target is one of its cells. The code looks up the seed table as <table>:Db whenever such a database table exists, and falls back to a task split only otherwise . The seeds are all rows whose target cell is present .

Autocomplete hides a trap: other columns of the same row can give the answer away. ShopDB’s review 1 reads “Terrible quality, broke within days.” and its rating is 1. So each autocomplete task lists leakage columns, which the sampler drops on the fly . For the paper’s rel-amazon rating task they are review_text and summary ; ShopDB’s rating task drops review_text.
An autocomplete seed: which cells become tokens

Pick a review and a task. The right side samples a real context with your L, w and RNG seed, then shows the seed row’s tokens. With reviews.rating the seed’s own review_text never enters; other reviews keep theirs unless they share the seed’s timestamp. With reviews.verified nothing is dropped, like the paper’s rel-amazon review.verified task .

No task rows appear in an autocomplete context, because the sampler follows task-table children only from a seed of that same task table . The in-context labels are the visible target values of other rows of the same table, such as other reviews of the same product. scaled down
In the official code
The rating of a rel-amazon review would leak through its text and summary, so both are dropped.

sections.title: Task-table prompting
blocks: This is the first of RT’s two innovations in input representation; the second, cell-level tokenization, is the subject of chapter 7 . “For each task, we attach a dedicated task table to the database. Only one task table is active at a time, ensuring that sampling is task-specific. Rows from the task table serve as seed rows for context construction, and from the model’s perspective task tables are treated as ordinary relational tables” . The paper calls it task-table prompting.
Attaching a task table to ShopDB
Attach either forecasting task. The task table joins the schema like any other table, with one foreign key to its entity, and its rows become children of that entity.

Why a table and not a special input? Because then a task lives in the same input space as pretraining: the model reads it through the same cells, column names and links as the rest of the database. In the paper’s words, task-table prompting “augments the database input with task-specific context, enabling zero-shot predictions across diverse schemas” , that is, predictions on a new database without weight updates . And since the task’s past rows carry their labels, the table also shows the model what answers look like for this entity and its neighbors .

In the code, “only one task table is active” works like this. Preprocessing indexes every task table of the database . The sampler then follows a link into a task table only when the seed belongs to that same table . A customer-churn seed never pulls in product-sales rows, and an autocomplete seed, being a database row, pulls in no task rows at all.
table_name_idx is shared by Train, Val and Test, so past rows of the same task pass the first test from any split; the second test is the temporal filter.

sections.title: What the model sees of a task row
blocks: Strip away the table and a task row is small. After preprocessing it has exactly two tokens: the timestamp cell (a datetime) and the label cell (a boolean or a number). The foreign key becomes a link, not a token: the entity’s node index goes into the row’s f2p_nbr_idxs list .
A task row becomes two tokens

From your live context: customer-churn, seed node 2406, L = 128, w = 16 scaled down. Hover a token for the value stored for the model. Both rows have the same two tokens; only the seed’s label is replaced by the mask.

Nothing tells the model which row holds the question. Every task row carries an is_task_node flag, but the model never reads it . The seed is special only because its label cell is the one masked token . The next chapter turns all these rows into numbers: which cells become tokens, and how each value is normalized (chapter 4).

sections.title: From rows to cells
blocks: Before the Relational Transformer sees anything, a preprocessing program runs once per database. It turns the database into one long list of rows, and every row into a few typed cells, with numbers, booleans and datetimes already normalized. This chapter follows that program on ShopDB, value by value.
How every row of every table, task splits included, gets one global node index.
Which values become cells: keys turn into links and missing values vanish.
How the physical dtype alone decides a cell’s semantic type.
Exactly how numbers, booleans and datetimes are z-scored, and which rows feed the statistics.
What one cell looks like after preprocessing, slot by slot.

sections.title: One program, run before everything else
blocks: RT never reads raw tables while it trains or predicts. The official code first runs a Rust program, pre.rs, once per database. It writes what the sampler needs: one record per row, the links between rows, every feature value already converted into numbers, and one string table that a separate script embeds with the frozen text encoder . It works in three passes.
Read the tables
Every parquet file, DB tables then task splits. Each file gets its node_idx_offset, which fixes every row’s global index.
read 1st here
Compute column statistics
Mean and standard deviation per number and boolean column; one global pair for all datetimes.
read 3rd here
Build the node vector
Per table, column by column over all rows: links and edges from foreign keys, one typed cell per non-missing feature value (z-scored with the pass-2 stats), and the string table.
read 2nd here
We take the passes in the order that is easiest to learn: the index space first, then which values become cells, then the statistics that normalize them.

Everything below is computed live in your browser, on ShopDB (e-commerce), by a TypeScript mirror of pre.rs: the same rows, links, cells and statistics. Its few bookkeeping differences are listed at the end of the chapter. The figures follow the simulation settings in the top bar, so the seed row you see here is the same one every other chapter uses: row 32 of customer-churn:Val, which points at customers[35] (Anna Müller).

sections.title: One index space for every row
blocks: pre.rs gives every row of every table a single integer, its global node index. “Every table” includes the task tables: the Train, Val and Test splits of each forecasting task are files of their own, and their rows are numbered in the same space as the database rows .

The order is simply the order in which the files are read: first the database tables db/*.parquet, sorted by path, then the task files tasks/<task>/<split>.parquet, sorted by path . Sorting by path compares the names byte by byte; for lowercase names like these, that is alphabetical order. That is why orders comes before products here, although the schema lists them the other way round, and why a task’s test split comes before its train split: test < train < val.

A file’s offset is the number of rows read before it, so a row’s index is node_idx_offset + its row position . The offsets are saved in table_info.json under keys like customers:Db or product-sales:Val .
ShopDB: 2,826 rows in 10 files, one index space

Press play to replay pass 1: pre.rs reads the files in glob order and each file’s offset is the running row count. Segments are colored by table; all task tables share magenta. The accent pin is the live seed row; the other pin follows the row picked below.

Why one shared space? The attention masks and the sampler compare rows only through these integers: “is this token in the same row as that one?”, “is that row one of my parents?” . One integer per row answers those questions the same way for every table. Note also what is not in the bar: autocomplete tasks add no table, because their seeds are ordinary database rows .
Lines 93-95 skip link-prediction tasks, whose directory names carry two extra dashes; RT cannot do link prediction (paper p.10 §7).

sections.title: Keys become links, missing values vanish
blocks: Inside a table, pre.rs walks the columns in their stored order and applies three rules to every value :
The primary key produces nothing: no cell and no edge . Its value is the row position, which the node index already encodes.

A foreign key produces no cell either. Its value becomes a link: the parent’s node index joins the row’s f2p_nbr_idxs, and the parent gets an edge back . This is also where the row’s timestamp is set, from its time column .
Every other value is a feature value. If it is present it becomes one cell record. If it is missing (null, or a float NaN) it produces nothing at all: no cell, no placeholder, no imputation .

The paper says the same in one line: once a row is selected, “all its non-missing feature cells (i.e., cells not from primary- or foreign-key columns) are included in the context” . Key columns shape the graph; only feature columns carry values.
One row through pass 3, column by column

Press play (or step) to watch each value land in its lane. The node record at the bottom fills up as pre.rs goes. pre.rs itself sweeps each column down all rows before it moves to the next column; here we follow one row’s slice of that sweep, which ends in the same node record. The signed numbers in the Cells lane are z-scores from pass 2 (see Normalization below): roughly, how many standard deviations a value sits above or below its column’s average. Picking another row here does not change the global seed.

These cell records are not tokens yet. A cell becomes a token only when the sampler picks its row for a context window (chapter 6). Even then one rule can skip it, and it belongs to the task, not to preprocessing: a task may name leakage columns, and the sampler leaves those cells out for the seed row and for every row with the seed’s timestamp (in ShopDB, reviews.rating drops review_text). pre.rs keeps those cells like any other. Across the whole database the rules add up as follows.

sections.title: Four semantic types, read off the dtype
blocks: Every cell carries a semantic type. There are four, with fixed codes from the SemType enum: Number = 0, Text = 1, DateTime = 2, Boolean = 3 . The model later loops over the types in exactly this order to pick an encoder, a mask vector and a decoder for each cell .
The type comes from the column’s physical dtype and from nothing else :
dtype → semantic type, with every feature column of ShopDB
Task-table columns appear once: the three splits share one table name and one column phrase.

There is no semantic inference. A string column is Text even when it is really a category, so a country code is embedded as a short string. An integer column that is not declared as a key is a Number, so a 1-to-5 rating is z-scored like a price, and an integer id that is not declared as a key would be too .

sections.title: Normalization: three kinds of z-score
blocks: Numbers, booleans and datetimes are stored as z-scores: subtract a mean, divide by a standard deviation. Text is not normalized at all; it is stored as an index into the database’s string table and embedded later by the frozen text encoder . There is no clipping anywhere. The paper writes the shared formula as
The three kinds differ only in which values feed μ and σ, and in how σ is computed.
Numbers: per column, sample standard deviation

For each number column, pre.rs drops nulls and NaNs, then takes the mean μ and the sample standard deviation σ, which divides by n − 1 (ddof = 1). Two guards keep the division safe: σ becomes 1 when it is undefined (n ≤ 1) or exactly 0 .

The z-score is a new ruler under the same data: 0 sits on the mean and one unit is one σ (the shaded band is μ ± σ). Bars are colored by table. Default probe: the seed’s own customer, where it applies.

The paper does not spell out why. Here is our reading, not a claim of the paper: one shared encoder per type, a Linear(1, d) with d = 256 in the paper and 64 here scaled down, reads every number column of every database . Standardizing first means it sees “how unusual is this value within its column” on a common scale, whether the column holds prices or ages.
Booleans: true lands above zero (when both values occur)

Booleans use the same formula after casting true → 1 and false → 0 . With a share p of trues, μ = p, so true becomes (1 − μ)/σ, which is positive, and false becomes −μ/σ, which is negative. The values are not ±1: they depend on how common true is, and a rare true sits far out on the positive side.

The sign is what the rest of the code relies on. The loss for a boolean target is binary cross-entropy against 1{z > 0}, and evaluation turns labels into int(z > 0) . Both read only the masked target cell , so “true ⇔ z > 0” must hold for every boolean column that can be a prediction target, and it does whenever both values occur . For the other boolean columns the sign has no special role: they are simply inputs.
Where true and false land on the z axis

Filled dot: true; hollow dot: false. Move the slider, or use the chips, to change how many values are true (n stays fixed); the dashed dots keep the real column for comparison. “All true” and “all false” show what a constant column does.
Datetimes: one clock for the whole database

Datetimes get no per-column statistics. Instead pre.rs pools every datetime value of every table, task splits included, into one count, one sum and one sum of squares. From them it derives a single mean μT and a population standard deviation σT, which divides by n (ddof = 0) and has no zero guard .
Each row is one datetime column of one table file. The accent triangle marked “seed” on the z ruler is the seed row’s timestamp.

The paper says to “normalize globally” but does not say why . One consequence follows from the code (our reading, not a claim of the paper): the same instant gets the same value in every column. A task row’s timestamp and an order’s time are on one scale, so the model can compare them directly.
Task labels: Train statistics for every split

Task tables get one extra step. pre.rs first computes stats for every file separately, then overwrites the Val and Test splits’ stats with the same task’s Train stats . A Val label is therefore normalized with the Train mean and σ, never with its own.
The split’s own label distribution differs from Train’s, but the μ and σ used are Train’s, so the same label is stored as the same value in every split.

For task labels the code does what the paper asks: statistics “computed on the training split” . The labels being evaluated do not shape their own encoding, and because the three splits share one table name and one column phrase (chapter 3), a Train label seen in the context and the Val label being predicted are on the same scale .

sections.title: Pick a cell, see its encoding
blocks: Here is the whole chapter in one panel. Click any cell of any table, task splits included. The panel walks it through pre.rs: its role, its semantic type, the statistics that normalize it, the record slots it fills, and the embedding term that will read it in chapter 8.
The cell inspector
Picking cells here is local to this figure; the global seed does not change.

Two details stand out in the slot view. Every cell record has all four value slots, and only the one that matches its type is filled; a non-text cell stores text index 0 . The model multiplies each type’s term by a 0/1 gate on the sem type, so the empty slots never contribute . And the seed’s own label is stored like any other cell: preprocessing knows nothing about masking. The sampler marks it as the target later, and the model swaps its value term for a learned mask vector .

sections.title: A note on precision
blocks: pre.rs stores number, datetime and boolean values as 32-bit floats . When the sampler builds a batch, it rounds number, datetime and boolean values to bfloat16, which keeps 8 significant bits, about two to three decimal digits . The paper runs pretraining and fine-tuning at BFloat16 precision ; the code also evaluates in bf16, with the labels for the loss and the metrics in bf16 too . This site keeps float32 everywhere.
The seed row and its entity, as this context window carries them

sections.title: Where this site’s mirror differs from pre.rs
blocks: Every cell value, link, timestamp and statistic in this chapter comes from a TypeScript mirror of pre.rs. It changes four pieces of bookkeeping, none of which changes what a token carries:
Time unit. Datetimes are stored in milliseconds instead of nanoseconds; the z-scores are the same (see the note in the datetime section).

String-table numbering. pre.rs walks its tables in hash-map order ; the mirror walks them in file order. So the text indices shown here (column phrases, table names, text values) are arbitrary labels that differ from the official ones. The model only compares them or looks up their embeddings, so the numbering carries no meaning .

Order of a parent’s child links. For the same reason, the P→F edges inside each parent’s list come in a different order . That changes only which random draw of the sampler picks which child (chapter 6), not which children can be picked.

Empty rows. A row with no non-null foreign key and no non-key column keeps pre.rs’s default header (node index 0) ; the mirror fills in its real index so the figures can label it. Such a row has no cells and no links, so it never yields a token.

2.A boolean column is true in 25% of its rows (n is large). What value does pre.rs store for true?

sections.title: Text and schema semantics
blocks: RT reads the names in a database. Every cell token carries a vector for the phrase “column of table”, made by a frozen sentence encoder, and every text value is embedded the same way. This chapter opens those vectors and asks how much they help a model move to a database it has never seen.
Which strings RT embeds, and the exact phrase “<col> of <table>”
What a real 384-dimensional all-MiniLM-L12-v2 vector looks like, and why its length is 1
How close the column phrases of ShopDB are to those of the pretraining databases
What it means that a text value is embedded without its column, and that the encoder is frozen
What the paper’s ablations say about the value of names
seed customer-churn:Val[32] → customers[35] (Anna Müller) · target phrase churn of customer-churn · 128 tokens use 17 distinct phrases scaled down

sections.title: Every cell carries the name of its column
blocks: RT describes a cell as a triple (v,c,t): its value, its column name and its table name . The value is normalized (numbers, dates and booleans; chapter 4) or embedded (text; Step 5) and becomes the token’s value term. The other two are joined into a short English phrase, “<column_name> of <table_name>”, and embedded by a frozen text encoder. The paper’s examples are “price of product” and “age of user”, and it calls this schema semantics . In the code, the phrase is one format string .

Every cell token carries the vector of its column phrase, whatever its type: a number, a date, a boolean, a string, and the masked target too . In the live context the target is the cell churn of customer-churn, so that phrase’s vector is part of the very token the model must fill in.
The column phrases of a database

Every phrase that preprocessing interns, grouped by table. Struck-through phrases belong to key columns: they get a string index but never a cell. Bars count the tokens of the live context that carry each phrase. Switching the database here does not change the live simulation.

Why a phrase rather than a column id? One of the paper’s three design principles is to “enable zero-shot generalization across heterogeneous schemas” . Our explanation of how a phrase serves it: an integer id means nothing outside its own database, while a phrase can be compared across databases. “age of customers” in ShopDB and “age of students” in SchoolDB are different columns, but they share words, and the encoder places them close together: cosine 0.53, against 0.13 for an average pair of phrases from different databases. Step 3 measures such closeness for every pair.

The primary-key and foreign-key columns get a phrase as well, because pre.rs interns the phrase before it checks the column’s role . But a primary key produces no cell, and a foreign key only becomes a link to the parent row . So customer_id of orders has a vector that no token ever uses. The paper lists this among RT’s limitations: it “does not incorporate the names of primary-key and foreign-key columns, which often carry useful semantics” .

The table name reaches a token only through the phrase. Each token also carries table_name_idx, but only as an integer: the column mask compares it , and the sampler uses it to recognize task tables . No vector is ever looked up through table_name_idx; a table name’s vector reaches a token only as the gated-out text[0] filler of Step 5 .
One string table per database

Preprocessing collects every string of a database into one list in order of first appearance: table names, column phrases and each distinct string value . It writes the list out as text.json . Identical strings share one index, and therefore one vector .
The string table of ShopDB

The first entries of the string table, in index order. Interning walks table by table and column by column, so names, phrases and values interleave. The order and the index numbers are this site’s: pre.rs visits the tables in hash-map order , so its text.json lists the same strings in another order. Indices are only ever compared for equality or used to fetch a string’s vector , so this changes nothing the model sees.
text_to_idx is the single string table of the database; an existing string keeps its index. column_name_to_idx becomes column_index.json.
The phrase is also how a task names its target. To find the column to mask, the training code looks up “<col> of <table>” in column_index.json .

sections.title: A real 384-dimensional vector
blocks: The text encoder is sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L12-v2 : a 12-layer BERT with hidden size 384 and a lower-casing WordPiece tokenizer . Its pipeline has three modules, Transformer → mean pooling → Normalize . In words: split the string into wordpieces, run all 12 layers to get one 384-dimensional vector per wordpiece, average them, and divide the average by its length.
Inside the encoder, for one string

Any of the 722 strings embedded offline for the four databases. The wordpieces come from the real tokenizer; the vector is the stored one. Hover a cell to read a dimension. The comparison rows show that the cosine of two unit vectors is the sum of their 384 element-wise products.

Two details in the figure deserve a look. First, words missing from the 30,522-entry vocabulary are split into smaller pieces, and every piece after the first is marked “##”; the target phrase becomes 9 wordpieces, [CLS] chu ##rn of customer - chu ##rn [SEP]. The encoder still returns one vector for the whole string. Second, the mean runs over every wordpiece, [CLS] and [SEP] included: we checked that this reproduces all stored vectors, and that leaving the two special tokens out does not.

Because of the final Normalize step, every vector has length 1 . All the information is in the direction, and the cosine similarity of two strings is simply their dot product. That is the measure Step 3 uses.

sections.title: Similarity across databases
blocks: One way names could help a pretrained model on a new database (our hypothesis; the paper does not test it): phrases of the new database would land near phrases with related meaning in the pretraining databases. Here every ShopDB phrase that can reach a token (rows) is compared with those of the other three databases (columns). Each cell is a cosine computed in your browser from the stored vectors.
Cosine similarity: ShopDB phrases vs the pretraining databases

Color runs from 0 to the legend’s maximum: the largest cosine shown, rounded up to 0.1. The ring marks each row’s best match. Rows are grouped by table, columns by database and then by table (named above each group, with the table’s color). On a narrow screen the cells scroll sideways under fixed row labels.

Take the label of the live task, churn of customer-churn. One might guess that its closest relatives are the labels of the pretraining databases’ tasks. The vectors say otherwise: the nearest pretraining phrase is reputation of users (cosine 0.385), a feature rather than a label; next comes engaged of user-engagement (0.318). The average over all 46 pretraining phrases is 0.133. Here is where each of their task labels ranks:

The encoder knows language, not databases. It places a phrase by its words and their everyday meaning, and the table name inside every phrase weighs on it as well. Over all four databases, two phrases of the same table average a cosine of 0.560, two phrases from different tables of one database 0.225, and two phrases from different databases 0.128. Whether a closeness like this is useful is not decided here: RT only receives these vectors as input, and pretraining decides what to make of them.

sections.title: A map of every column phrase
blocks: To see all 99 column phrases of the four databases at once, we project their vectors onto the two directions along which they vary most (a principal component analysis, computed offline from the same stored vectors). Two axes cannot hold 384 dimensions: they keep 18% of the variance, so nearby points are not always near neighbors. Pin a phrase to draw its true nearest neighbors, measured in all 384 dimensions.
Column phrases of the four databases, 2-D PCA

Color and shape mark the database. Hollow markers are key columns (interned, never on a token). Dashed lines join the pinned phrase to its five nearest phrases in 384-d. Click a database chip to hide it.

In this projection, the key-column phrases sit at an average PC 1 of +0.35, the other phrases at −0.18. The full 384-d vectors agree that the “…_id of …” phrases form a group: two key-column phrases average a cosine of 0.436, a key-column phrase and another phrase 0.156, two other phrases 0.163. Along PC 2 the databases spread out, from SchoolDB (average +0.32) to ShopDB (−0.29). In 384-d, two phrases from different tables of one database average 0.225, two phrases from different databases 0.128. Our reading: the phrases of a database share its table names and domain words. RT never computes this map; it is only a window onto the vectors it receives.

sections.title: Text cells: the raw value, nothing else
blocks: String values go through the same encoder, applied to the raw string with nothing added: r=Etext(v) . Preprocessing interns the value string itself , the encoder embeds that list , and the sampler copies the row into the token’s text_values . The column never becomes part of the string . In the live context, the customer’s value “DE” is embedded as exactly that string.
Two vectors per text token
Pick a text cell of the live context. The token holds two separate rows of the string table: its column phrase and its raw value.

The column context of a text cell therefore comes only from the separate column term . Inside the model, each vector passes through its own linear layer and RMSNorm, and the two results are added ; chapter 8 follows that sum.
One string, one index, in every column

In SchoolDB, “Computer Science” is a value of both program of students and department of courses. pre.rs interns it once, as text[28], so both cells carry the very same value vector. Only their column vectors differ (cosine 0.552).
5 such strings across the four databases: “Computer Science”, “Biology”, “History”, “Mathematics”, “Economics”

What about cells that are not text? Preprocessing stores text index 0 for them , so the sampler copies the vector of text[0] into their text_values as well. text[0] is always a table name, the first one pre.rs interns: in our preprocessing of ShopDB it is “customers”, while pre.rs’s hash order may put another table first. The model multiplies that term by zero, because the token’s sem type is not text .
Long strings would be cut: the encoder truncates at 128 wordpieces . The longest string in our four databases has 21 wordpieces, [CLS] and [SEP] included, so nothing is cut here.
val is the cell’s string as it is: no column name, no table name. col_name_idx (line 603) is stored separately.

sections.title: Why names matter
blocks: The paper tests the value of names directly. It shuffles the column and table names in the context and measures performance with the same pretrained checkpoints . “For zero-shot evaluation, the ablations are applied directly to the sampled context used as input. For fine-tuning, models are trained to convergence with the same modified contexts” . The paper does not describe the shuffling procedure in more detail. In the same table it removes two kinds of labels from the context, which gives a yardstick for the names.
Mean over the RelBench tasks for each context ablation (paper Table 4, p.9)

In the paper’s words, “the model indeed leverages table/column names for zero-shot transfer, as wrong names lead to consistent degradation. After full fine-tuning, context ablations have little effect” (the exception it names is self labels on regression) . Appendix G adds that shuffling names “also harms transfer, highlighting the importance of semantic signals from schema metadata” . On average, zero-shot AUROC falls by 0.6 points and R² by 2.3 points. Removing the target entity’s past labels costs 16.3 and 28.3: in the paper’s words, “zero-shot transfer is driven primarily by the model’s ability to leverage past labels of the target entity” . Names are a consistent but smaller signal. One way to read the zero-shot versus fine-tuned difference (ours, not the paper’s): a fine-tuned model has seen many labeled examples of the task and can learn what each column means from its values, while a zero-shot model must rely more on what the names say.

The mean hides spread. In zero-shot, shuffling lowers the score on 7 of the 10 binary tasks and 7 of the 8 regression tasks. The largest drops are rel-hm user-churn (−2.8 AUROC) and rel-stack post-votes (−4.9 R²), while rel-stack user-engage gains +3.0 .
The paper’s conclusion ranks what drives zero-shot transfer . Names come fourth of five, after the target entity’s past labels, which matches the gap between their two rows in Table 4:
forecasting from the target entity’s past task rows;
column attention;
feature attention, in the same and in parent tables;
schema semantics from table and column names;
in-context learning from other entities’ task rows.
Not lexical copying

Could the model simply match identical column names across databases? The paper checks with the Jaccard overlap of the column names of two databases: the number of shared names divided by the number of distinct names in the two databases together, ∣A∩B∣ / ∣A∪B∣. Between RelBench databases it is tiny, at most 0.043 (rel-amazon vs rel-hm), and fuzzy string matching gives only 0.47 to 0.59 . Its conclusion: “RT’s zero-shot generalization cannot be attributed to lexical similarity. Instead, the model must learn to recognize and exploit structural relational patterns” .

The paper does not say how names help, then. Two readings fit its results (ours, not the paper’s). Names may carry meaning across databases through the encoder, as Step 3 measures. Or they may mainly tell columns apart within one context, the role App. E describes. The shuffle ablation removes both, so Table 4 cannot separate them.
Column-name overlap (Jaccard) between databases

Jaccard overlap = shared column names / distinct column names of the two databases. Left: the paper’s numbers. Right: the same statistic on this site’s four toy databases, computed live. The paper does not say which columns it counted; we count every column of the database tables (keys included, task tables excluded). Hover a cell for the counts and the shared names.

sections.title: The encoder is frozen
blocks: RT never runs its text encoder while it trains or predicts. embed.py embeds the whole string table once and writes the vectors to a file . The sampler memory-maps that file and copies rows by index . So no gradient can reach the encoder. The first trainable parameters on the text path are two linear maps from 384 to d, enc_dict["col_name"] and enc_dict["text"], each followed by its own RMSNorm .
Where the text vectors come from, and where learning starts

The paper describes the encoder as frozen without discussing the choice: “a frozen text encoder” , “frozen language model (LM) embeddings of table/column names” . Three consequences follow from the design. Training never pays for the encoder: each step reads precomputed rows. A new database needs one pass of the encoder over its strings, and no change to RT. And a string has the same vector in every database, so the similarities of Step 3 are fixed facts that pretraining can learn to use.

sections.title: Why sample?
blocks: RT reads a database as a set of cell tokens, and a whole database does not fit in one sequence. ShopDB (e-commerce) is tiny by RelBench standards, yet the tables this task’s sampler may enter hold 7,019 feature cells. So for every prediction RT builds a short sequence around one seed row: the context window of L cells . Here the seed row is customer-churn Val row 32 (customer 35, 2025-03-01), and its masked cell is the label to predict.

Which L cells? The authors follow “the intuition that most relevant information lies within a few hops of the seed row when following F→P and P→F links, and that lower hops are more informative than higher hops” . A plain search cannot keep all of them: the chart counts the cells within k hops of the seed, and already at 2 hops there are more than L = 128.

sections.title: The algorithm, one decision at a time
blocks: The paper describes the sampler as a breadth-first search with three changes: all parent rows (F→P) are always included, child rows (P→F) are subsampled with a BFS width bound w, and rows with timestamps later than the seed row are excluded. Once a row is selected, its non-missing feature cells are added to the context .

The released implementation, rustler/src/fly.rs, keeps the frontier in two structures: an F→P stack for parent rows and a list of P→F depth buckets for child rows . Every frontier entry carries a depth label, one more than the depth of the row that pushed it . The visited check happens when an entry is taken off the frontier, not when it is pushed, so duplicates can wait in the frontier and are skipped later .

sections.title: Four rules worth remembering
blocks: Strip away the bookkeeping and the released sampler follows four rules, among them the temporal filter and the width bound w. Each card shows its rule at work in the context above; “Show me” moves the replay to that moment.
Each rule differs in a detail from the paper’s description, and each card says how. The code is what produced the released model, so this course follows the code .
Parents first, always, never filtered
Whenever the F→P stack is non-empty, its top is popped: no randomness, no time filter, no width bound, and the last foreign key pushed is followed first.
51 parent pushes, 52 stack pops (38 of them already visited). order 70 pushed customer 35 then product 4; product 4 was on top, so it was popped first and visited.
Children only if not later than the seed

A P→F child is skipped only when both timestamps exist and the child’s is later than the seed’s. Equal timestamps pass, rows without a timestamp pass, and the comparison is always against the seed, never the current row.
263 child rows skipped as too late. First one: order 967 at 2025-03-05, after the seed’s 2025-03-01.
At most w DB children per row; task rows never subsampled

If more than w of a row’s DB children pass the time filter, a uniform random w of them is kept (without replacement). Children from the seed’s task table that pass the time filter bypass the bound: all of them enter the frontier.
The bound fired 11 times; the largest cut: product 4 had 277 DB children after the time filter, 16 kept. 50 customer-churn rows entered the frontier without any subsampling.
Stop at exactly L cells
The loop breaks as soon as the L-th token is written, even in the middle of a row. If the frontier empties first, the rest is padding.
Full at L = 128: customer 44 was cut after 1 of its 4 cells.
One more filter exists for autocomplete tasks only: their leakage columns are skipped for the seed row and for rows with the seed’s timestamp . Forecasting tasks such as customer-churn drop nothing .

sections.title: In-context labels
blocks: The task table is attached to the database as an ordinary table , so the search can walk into it. The path is short: the seed row pushes its entity onto the stack (depth 1), and the entity’s children go to bucket 2. Those children are the entity’s DB rows, time-filtered and cut to w, plus every row of the same task table in any split whose timestamp is not later than the seed’s, never subsampled . Their label cells are not masked: they are in-context labels.

The paper is careful to say this is not few-shot prompting: “While task rows provide ‘in-context labels’, our setting is not few-shot as explicit subgraph-label pairs are not required” . The model receives labels only as ordinary cells of the context.
In the context of customer-churn Val row 32 (customer 35, 2025-03-01), customer 35 contributes 12 self labels, its own past churn values, and other entities contribute 0.
Labels the model can read, on a time axis
Top: label rows by time; everything right of the seed line is later than the seed and is never sampled . Bottom: the same label cells among all L tokens.

Other entities’ labels arrive by longer paths, for example entity → one of its transactions → the product it points to (F→P) → another transaction of that product → its customer (F→P) → that customer’s task rows . Each hop adds one to the depth label, and the lowest bucket is always drawn first, so these rows wait until the shallower buckets are empty . With w = 16 this context holds none, so the figures offer a second context of the same seed: with w = 3, every bucket is smaller, and the search reaches other entities within L = 128 cells.
How each label entered the context
For every label row of the context, the path through which the search visited it, drawn with foreign-key arrows (child → parent).

Which task rows can appear depends on the seed’s split. All three splits share one table name, so the task-table test lets every split through, and the time filter keeps every row with a timestamp no later than the seed’s :
a Train seed sees Train rows up to its own timestamp;
a Val seed sees all Train rows, plus other entities’ Val rows at the same timestamp;
a Test seed sees Train and Val rows, plus other entities’ Test rows at the same timestamp.
Visibility of customer-churn rows by seed split
Your seed is a Val row. A seed’s own row is the masked target; the rows of other entities at the same timestamp are the “same horizon” rows.
How many labels does the paper see?

For scale, the paper counts the labels in 1024-cell contexts of its tasks. Note rel-trial study-outcome and study-adverse: no labels at all, and zero-shot AUROC on study-outcome is 51.8, close to random .

Self labels are the main driver of zero-shot transfer. Removing them drops the paper’s mean zero-shot AUROC from 70.1 (Table 4’s baseline; Table 1’s re-run headline mean is 69.7) to 53.8, and R² from 22.8 to −5.5, while removing other-entity labels changes little (70.6 and 22.9) . In the authors’ words, “zero-shot transfer is driven primarily by the model’s ability to leverage past labels of the target entity” .

One caveat on provenance: Table 4 is unchanged since the paper’s first arXiv version, so it predates the released sampler. At that time the public sampler still excluded same-horizon task rows, so Table 4 does not measure the effect of the same-horizon labels the released code shows .

Two mechanisms are at work. A bucket is drawn uniformly, so the self labels in bucket 2 compete with the entity’s DB children for the first positions: with a large w more DB children share that bucket, and a small L can fill up before every self label is drawn . The paper varied L at inference for a model pretrained at L = 1024 and found that “RT’s performance degrades gracefully, showing a drop of only 4% absolute AUROC and 7% absolute R² with 25% lower time and 20% lower memory” (Fig. 4, from L = 1024 down to 256). sections.title: The batch dictionary
blocks: The sampler of chapter 6 does not hand the model a table or a graph. It writes the context into parallel arrays, one slot per position. In fly.rs a struct holds one vector per field , every slot starts as padding , and each emitted cell fills position seq_i of every field . On the Python side, data.py turns the buffers into tensors of shape [B, S] (ids, types and flags), [B, S, 1] (the scalar value slots), [B, S, 5] (the parent lists) or [B, S, 384] (embeddings) . That dictionary of tensors is the batch dictionary .

B counts sequences: 32 per GPU in the paper’s runs . S is the context length L. One sequence is one context window, so on this page B = 1 and S = 128. Each position holds one cell token, or padding. Open any position below to see its record.
The batch dictionary of the live context: 128 positions

Top: one square per position, in the order the sampler emitted the cells. Middle: where the inspected token comes from, and every field the model receives for it. Bottom: the whole batch dictionary as one table, one row per position (open it with the toggle). The inspected token is shared with the embedding, masks and attention chapters.

The fields fall into four groups, and the figure follows them. The ids say which cell a token is: which row (node_idxs), which parent rows (f2p_nbr_idxs), which table and which column (table_name_idxs, col_name_idxs). The four attention masks are built from these ids and from is_padding, and from nothing else . The content fields say what the cell holds: the embedding of its column phrase, its semantic type and one value slot per type. The input embedding reads them . Three flags mark the masked target and the padding. Two fields ride along unused: is_task_nodes and class_value_idxs are written by the sampler but never read by the paper-era model .

Watch out for one name clash. The batch field masks marks the one hidden cell (Step 3). The four attention masks of chapter 9 are something else: S × S tables of allowed pairs, built from the ids . The figure tags a field “attention masks” when those tables read it.

Every token carries all four value slots, but only the one that matches its sem_types counts. The code computes every type’s value term and multiplies the others by 0 . The unused number, datetime and boolean slots hold 0, and text_values of a non-text cell holds the embedding of text[0], whatever string has index 0 in the database’s string table (here “customers”) .
true_batch_size is per batch, not per token: it counts the real sequences of a wrapped last batch and is used only in evaluation (spec §4.14).
seq_i is the next free position. The row-level fields (node, parents, table) are copied from the node for every one of its cells.
Every field is reshaped to [B, S], [B, S, 5], [B, S, 1] or [B, S, 384]. The value fields arrive as raw bf16 bytes.

sections.title: Rows are not tokens, cells are
blocks: RT samples rows but tokenizes cells. The paper calls this cell-level tokenization: “each database cell is modeled as an individual token” . Rows remain the sampling unit: once a row is selected, its non-missing feature cells enter the context . In the live context, orders[70] becomes 3 tokens.

What ties k separate tokens back into one row? Ids. Each token repeats its row’s node_idxs, f2p_nbr_idxs and table_name_idxs . The feature mask uses the shared node id to let the cells of a row read each other, and the parent ids to let them read their parent rows . The neighbor mask uses the same parent ids in the other direction . A token that did not carry its row’s id and parents could not take part in those layers.
One row in, k tokens out

Top: the raw row, column by column, and what becomes of each value. Bottom: the row’s tokens as the model receives them. Shaded bars are the row-level fields, written again for every cell; the per-cell fields differ from token to token. The masked target still stores its label (lock icon), which the input embedding gates out (Step 3). E(“…”) is the frozen MiniLM embedding of a string (chapter 5). Click a token number to inspect it in Step 1.

The key columns never become tokens. The primary key column is skipped . The node id comes from the row’s position instead: each table gets an offset, the number of rows of the tables loaded before it , and a row’s node id is that offset plus its position . That position equals the key in RelBench-style data, where keys are 0 … n−1 in row order . Each foreign key value is turned into a node id the same way, with the parent table’s offset, and becomes a parent id in f2p_nbr_idxs . A missing value produces no token at all .
The parent list

f2p_nbr_idxs always has five slots. The sampler asserts that no row has more than MAX_F2P_NBRS = 5 parents and writes them into the first slots . The other slots keep the −1 they were allocated with . The list holds all of the row’s parents, in foreign-key column order, whether or not they made it into the context. A parent can only change attention if some of its cells are present .

In practice the parents are almost always there. When the sampler visits a row it pushes the row’s parents on its F→P stack , which has priority over everything else . So they, and their own parents in turn, are visited before any child row. The stack is last in, first out, so the parent of the last foreign key comes first .A listed parent ends up without tokens only if the hard stop at L comes first, or if the parent row has no non-null feature cell to emit . In the live context, every parent listed by any token is in the context.

sections.title: Exactly one masked cell
blocks: Exactly one token of a context has masks = true: the target cell of the seed row. The sampler sets is_target when the row is the seed and the column is the target column, and copies it into masks . There is no random masking anywhere in the paper-era sampler or model; training and evaluation build sequences the same way . Every other cell is visible, including other rows’ values of the target column: the in-context labels of chapter 6 (here 12 labels of the seed’s own entity and none of other entities).
The masks field of the live context
The array exactly as the model receives it: one boolean per position. Hover a cell to see which token it belongs to. The single true entry is the seed row’s target cell .

The masked token is not removed and not blanked. It keeps its row and parent ids, its column phrase and its type, so the model knows which column of which table it must fill, and in which row . Only the value term of its input embedding changes: instead of encoding the value, the model adds a learned mask vector for the cell’s type . Chapter 8 computes it with real numbers.
The masked target next to a visible label of the same column

Left: the target, customer-churn:Val[32]. Right: a past label of the same entity, customer-churn:Train[564] = false. Table, column and type match, so both tokens get the same column-name term and the same encoder. They differ in row id. Of the flags the model reads, only masks differs, and it swaps the value term for the mask vector . Click a column header to inspect that token in Step 1.
The label is still in the arrays

Here is a detail that surprises most readers. The sampler writes the value of every emitted cell, the target included . The true label of the seed row (churn = false) therefore sits in the target token’s boolean_values slot, in plain sight. It cannot leak. The input embedding still computes this value’s term, then multiplies it by the gate [sem = t ∧ ¬mask ∧ ¬pad], which is 0 for the target . The square brackets are a 0/1 switch: 1 if the condition inside holds, 0 otherwise. The label has an effect in only two places: the loss uses it as its target , and the evaluation uses it as the label for the metrics .

Try it. Replace the stored label and run the model again. The rerun below does not take the site engine’s shortcut of skipping a term whose gate is 0: it computes every term from the arrays, hidden label included, and multiplies it by its gate, as the code does.
Experiment: overwrite the hidden label

The forward pass runs again in your browser on the same 128 tokens, with only the target’s stored value replaced. This rerun evaluates the input embedding literally, the way writes it: at every position the value term of every type is computed from its slot, the replaced label included, multiplied by its gate and added up. That input then passes through the four blocks. The prediction is read at the masked position, as evaluation does , and the loss uses the stored value as its target . The bottom panel opens the gate for the target alone.

The prediction does not move by a single bit, while the loss can. For a boolean target the loss reads only the sign of the stored value, 1{z > 0}, so any positive number gives the same loss as “true” . That is the contract of the masked cell: its value is invisible to the model, yet available to grade it .
Line 219 keeps a value term only where the token is not masked and not padding. Line 223 adds the mask vector exactly where it is masked.
y is the same value array the input gate ignored; sem_type_mask keeps only the masked position.

sections.title: No positional encodings
blocks: A language model must tell “dog bites man” from “man bites dog”, so it adds positional encodings to its tokens. RT leaves them out on purpose: “To preserve the natural symmetries of relational data, RT does not incorporate positional encodings” . A table has no first row and no first column, and the paper wants a model that is “invariant to permutations of rows, columns, and tables” .

Nothing in the code depends on where a token sits. Its input vector is computed from its own fields only: column phrase, type, value, and the mask and padding flags, never its index . The four attention masks compare ids and padding flags only . Shuffle the tokens and each one gets the same input vector and the same set of allowed keys as before, at a new index. Write the shuffle as a permutation matrix P acting on the rows of the token matrix X; the masks M become PMP⊤, and the final hidden states H are permuted the same way :
Shuffle the inputs, and the outputs come out shuffled the same way, each one unchanged.

The hidden states are equivariant: each one moves with its token. The prediction is read at the target, wherever it lands, so it is invariant. Our reading: inside the model, this token-order invariance is what the paper’s claim comes down to, since the model never sees in which order the sampler wrote the cells. In exact arithmetic the equality is exact. In floating point, a different order of the keys can change the order of the sums and so the last bits; the official model runs FlexAttention in bfloat16 , where equality holds up to rounding. Do not take it on faith: shuffle the live context and run the model again.
Experiment: shuffle the tokens, run the model again

Each square is one token (color = table, “?” = the masked target). Shuffling moves the squares to random positions: the token arrays are permuted, the four masks are rebuilt from the permuted ids , and the full forward pass runs again in your browser. Mathematically the result is exact. In floating point a different key order can change the last bits, so the official bfloat16 model gives equality up to rounding. This site’s engine adds up its dot products and weighted sums in 64-bit floats and stores 32-bit results (src/engine/model/ops.ts), so a different summation order moves the sums far below what a 32-bit float can hold, and the comparison reports what it actually gets. Focus the squares and use the arrow keys to follow one token.

sections.title: Padding
blocks: Every sequence of a batch has the same length, so the sampler allocates batch_size × seq_len slots up front and gives each one a padding default: node −1, parents −1, table and column 0, every value 0, is_padding = true . Emitting a cell overwrites its slot and sets is_padding = false . A context ends in one of two ways . Either the sampler reaches exactly L cells and stops, even in the middle of a row , or the frontier runs out of rows first and the remaining slots stay padding.
Padding: the slots the sampler never wrote

Top: the is_padding array and the tokens of a context that ran out of rows. Left: one padding slot, every field at the value Vecs::new gave it. Right: what the model does with it, computed from the real weights and masks of this context.

Padding is inert by construction. Every mask is ANDed with “neither token is padding” , and every term of the input embedding is multiplied by ¬is_padding , so a padding slot stays 0 through every block . The last check in the figure is the consequence that matters: the same cells give the same prediction with or without the padding slots around them .

sections.title: The token embedding
blocks: Before any attention happens, every cell token becomes one vector of d numbers, x₀. It is the sum of two parts: a term that says which column of which table the cell belongs to, and a term that says what value it holds. The masked target gets a trainable mask vector in place of its value. This chapter computes x₀ for the live context, number by number.
