sections.title: Two terms per token
blocks: The previous chapter turned every cell into a cell token: a column phrase, a semantic type, a stored value and a few integer ids . The ids only steer the attention masks of the next chapter. Everything the transformer learns about a cell’s content enters through one vector per token, the input embedding xi∈Rd, with d = 64 here and 256 in the paper .
The code builds it as follows :
Read it one piece at a time.

The column term says where the cell lives. ci is the frozen MiniLM embedding of its column phrase “<column> of <table>”, for example “churn of customer-churn” . One linear layer Wcol serves every column of every table.

The value term says what the cell holds. vi(t) is the value slot of type t: a single z-score for numbers, datetimes and booleans, and the 384-d MiniLM embedding of the string for text . The sampler fills all four slots of every cell; the gate keeps the one of the cell’s type . Each type has its own linear layer Wt and its own RMSNorm.
The mask vector mt takes the value term’s place for the masked target. It is a trainable parameter, one per type, and is added as it is, with no norm .
The square brackets are 0/1 gates. For a real token exactly one of the eight value-side gates is 1. For a padding token every gate is 0, the column gate included, so its x₀ is the zero vector .

Here are those gates for all 128 positions of the live context. Every real token takes the column term and exactly one of the eight value-side gates: most take a value encoder, and exactly one, the target, takes a mask vector .

sections.title: Follow one token through
blocks: The figure below computes x₀ for one token in seven stages, ① to ⑦. The left lane is the column term, the right lane the value term or the mask vector, and stage ⑦ adds them. Every strip holds real numbers from the forward pass of the checkpoint this page runs; hover a 64-d strip to see the arithmetic of a single dimension.

Stages ③ and ⑥ are RMSNorms. An RMSNorm divides a vector by its root mean square, plus a small constant ε inside the square root, and multiplies it by a learned gain γ . Step 3 looks at it closely; for now, the panel next to each norm shows the numbers it uses.

The figure opens on the token you last inspected, the masked target by default. It plays once when it scrolls into view; replay it or try the presets. A few things to notice. Two cells of the same column get the same column term. A text value goes through MiniLM on its own, without its column name . For the masked target, stages ⑤ and ⑥ do nothing: its mask vector goes straight into the sum.
Compute x₀ for one token of the live context

Pick any token: click a square, or a preset; in the strip the arrow keys move and Enter picks. The seven stages follow model.py:208-224, with the weights of the checkpoint this page runs. The player stays at the top of the screen while you scroll through the stages. Hover a cell of any 64-d strip to see the arithmetic of that dimension in every stage. Post-norm vectors (③, ⑥, ⑦) share one color scale; the others have their own (shown as “scale ±…”).

The code does not branch on the type. It evaluates all four value branches at every position, then multiplies each by its gate . Every slot holds something, because the sampler writes all of them . Every slot must also hold a finite number, because the branches are evaluated before the multiplication by the gate, and NaN·0 = NaN . A non-text cell’s text_values slot, for example, holds the embedding of text index 0, a table name, which the gate then zeroes . Our engine skips the branches whose gate is 0, which gives the same sum for any finite value .
col_name_values gets the phrase embedding; all three scalar slots and the text slot are written for every cell, whatever its type.
The trailing 1 is why a scalar can go through nn.Linear(1, d).

sections.title: RMSNorm, and why its ε matters here
blocks: Each projection in the embedding is followed by an RMSNorm. It divides a vector by its root mean square and then multiplies dimension j by a learned gain γj :

There is no mean subtraction and no bias: only a division and a per-dimension gain. With γ = 1, which is how every gain starts , the output keeps the input’s direction and has a root mean square close to 1, unless the input is tiny.

The small constant ε keeps the division safe. The code calls nn.RMSNorm(d_model) without an ε. In the paper’s pinned environment (torch 2.6 with bfloat16 tensors) PyTorch then uses the bfloat16 machine epsilon, 2−7 . This site uses the same value.
RMSNorm in two dimensions: drag the input
Around the origin, magnified ×7

The output y is computed by the same RMSNorm kernel the engine uses, with d = 2. The dashed curve is where y lands when ε is negligible: the circle of radius √2 (rms = 1) stretched by γ. The shaded disk is the ε zone, mean(x²) < ε: inside it ε is most of the sum under the square root; the magnified view shows it at a readable size. Drag x into it, use the arrow keys after focusing the handle (Shift for bigger steps), or try the column-projection preset. The plane widens when a γ needs the room.

In d dimensions the same thing happens on a sphere. With γ = 1 the output length is ∥y∥=d⋅r/r2+ε, where r is the input’s root mean square. When r2≫ε that is d, 8 here and 16 in the paper. When r2 is comparable to ε, the output stays shorter, because RMSNorm can scale a vector up by at most 1/ε≈11.3. And RMSNorm(0⃗)=0⃗ exactly.
Where ε takes over, with the real inputs of the five RMSNorms

Top: the length RMSNorm gives a vector (as rms, before γ) as a function of the length it receives. Bottom: every distinct input of the live forward pass, one dot each, placed by its rms. Left of √ε, ε is more than half of the sum under the root and the output keeps less than 71% of its full length; well to the right (r ≫ √ε) it reaches full length. Hover or tap a dot for its numbers; click it (or focus it and press Enter) to inspect that token in Step 2.

Now the real inputs. In the checkpoint this page runs, Wcolc+bcol has a median mean square of 0.0028 over the 17 column phrases of this context, and all 17 of them are below ε = 0.0078. For a typical phrase, ε makes up 74% of mean(x²) + ε, the sum under the square root. So the column terms come out about 3.3 long, while number value terms reach about 7.1. ε is not the only reason: training also left γcol the smallest of the five gains (∥γcol∥ = 6.33, against 7.04 for γnumber; all ones would give 8).

This matters for what the model sees. In this checkpoint a number value term is about 2.2 times as long as a column term, so x₀ is dominated by the value. Two cells with the same z in different columns therefore start out with similar x₀; Step 4 measures how similar. What tells them apart is the shorter column component, and the attention layers have to work with that.

Why the column projection starts small follows from the default initialization, in our model and in the paper’s alike. PyTorch draws every weight and bias of nn.Linear(384, d) uniformly from ±1/384 , and c has length 1 . Each output dimension then has E[xj2]=(∥c∥2+1)/(3⋅384)=1/576≈0.0017, whatever d is: about 0.22 ε. Our exported initial weights give a median of 0.0016 for this context’s phrases. The spec notes the same order of magnitude, mean(x²) ≈ 2·10⁻³ . How far training moves it in the paper’s 256-d model is not reported.
The gains γ are the only parameters of an RMSNorm. The embedding has five of them, one per projection, each with 64 entries .
The five learned gains γ, one dot per dimension
Each RMSNorm multiplies its output by its own γ (64 numbers), which starts at 1 in every dimension (the dashed line). Training moved them in our mini model; this is the checkpoint the page runs.

sections.title: One encoder per type, shared by every column
blocks: A number, a datetime or a boolean enters as one scalar z, the z-score computed in preprocessing . Its encoder is nn.Linear(1, d): one weight column wt∈Rd and a bias bt . So the value term is

As z changes, z wt+bt moves along a straight line in Rd. RMSNorm moves every point of that line onto the sphere of radius √d (nearly, because of ε), and γ stretches the result. All values of one type therefore live on a single one-dimensional curve .

The encoder belongs to the type, not to the column. Age of customers, price of products, quantity of orders and rating of reviews all go through enc_dict["number"] . Two cells with the same z get exactly the same value term, whichever column they come from. What tells them apart in x₀ is the column term .
Move a value along its type’s curve: RMSNorm_number(z·w + b)

The curve is RMSNorm_number(z·w + b) for z from −3 to 3, computed with the weights of the checkpoint this page runs and drawn in its own two main directions (PCA, 100% of its variance). Hollow dots: every distinct stored value of the selected column; hover, tap or focus one for its value, click or press Enter to move there. × marks the limits z → ±∞. Every number column of every table lands on this same curve.

The flat picture loses nothing. z wt+bt always lies in the plane spanned by wt and bt; RMSNorm only slides each point along its own ray, and γ is a linear map. So the whole curve lies in one plane, which is why its first two principal directions capture all of it. As z runs from −∞ to +∞, the direction of z wt+bt turns from −wt to +wt: before γ the curve is half of a circle of radius about √d, and γ stretches it into half of an ellipse. All of this follows from the formula alone.

Two more consequences follow. First, a z-score is the only thing the value term sees, and a z-score counts standard deviations of its own column . So z = 0.5 means “half a standard deviation above the mean age” in one column and “half a standard deviation above the mean price” in another; the column term has to carry the difference. Second, for very large |z| the bias becomes negligible next to z wt, so the curve flattens out toward the two points marked × in the figure, as its cosine chart shows: extreme values of a type all look alike.

Text works differently. Its encoder is nn.Linear(384, d) on the string’s MiniLM vector, so text values do not lie on one curve: each distinct string is its own point . Like the column term, it starts from a unit-length MiniLM vector . Step 3’s figure shows where the text values of this context land relative to √ε.

sections.title: The mask vector
blocks: The seed row’s target cell is the only masked token in a context . Its value term is replaced by mt, a trainable vector of the target’s type, created as nn.Parameter(torch.randn(d_model)) . It skips both the linear layer and the RMSNorm .

So the masked token still knows a lot. Its column term names the column and the table, its mask vector names the type, and its ids tie it to its row and to the entity it is about . It does not know its value. The attention layers have to fill that in from the rest of the context.
The four mask vectors, and what the masked target still knows

Left: mask_embs of the checkpoint this page runs, on one shared color scale, each compared with its value in the exported initial weights. Right: the live masked target, and what the code does with its hidden label.

The label is still in the batch. The sampler writes the true value into the target’s slot like any other cell, and only is_targets and masks mark it . The gate ¬maski keeps it out of x₀; the loss reads it later as the training target .

sections.title: Padding is the zero vector
blocks: When the sampler runs out of rows before L tokens, the remaining positions are padding. Every field keeps the default it was created with, and is_padding stays true . Every term of x₀ is multiplied by ¬padi, so a padding token’s input is exactly zero .
A padding token, as the sampler initializes it
The live context fills all 128 positions, so it has no padding. This token is built from the sampler’s defaults and embedded by the same engine function as the live context.
It stays zero all the way through. Every attention mask excludes padding, a fully masked attention row outputs 0, the feed-forward network maps 0 to 0, and RMSNorm(0⃗)=0⃗ .
A cell overwrites these defaults (fly.rs:462-500); a slot no cell reaches keeps them.

What sets them apart is a boolean mask that decides which token may look at which. This chapter builds the four masks for the live context and shows what each one lets through.

sections.title: Attention with a mask
blocks: Inside every attention layer, RT computes standard scaled dot-product attention. Each token’s query vector is compared with every key vector, the scores pass through a softmax, and the resulting weights average the value vectors . Each of the four layers has its own query, key, value and output weights and its own RMSNorm . What sets the four layers apart is the attention mask M∈{0,1}n×n: M[q,k]=1 means that token q may attend to token k, and 0 means it cannot .

You may know masks from GPT-style language models, which use the causal mask Mcausal[q,k]=1{k≤q} so that no token reads the tokens after it . RT has no causal mask: its attention is bidirectional, and its masks are built from row, column and table ids, so they say nothing about token order . They encode relations instead.

A word on names. Paper Figure 1 brackets the column, feature and neighbor layers as the Relational Attention layers, and the fourth, full attention, is unrestricted (App. J uses the name for all four ). This chapter says “the three relational masks” for the first three and “the four masks” when full is included.
Scaled dot-product attention with masking, as printed in the paper (v3).

The mask acts before the softmax. A blocked pair gets the score −∞, and e−∞=0, so the softmax shares all of the weight among the allowed keys as if the blocked ones did not exist. Rows are queries and columns are keys; every matrix in this chapter is drawn that way.

The figure uses the real scores of the trained mini model at the masked target. It lets you pick one of the three relational layers, which Step 2 defines; for now, watch only what happens to the blocked keys. Tokens are labeled row·column: val32 is the seed row customer-churn:Val[32] and c35 is customers[35].
Where the masked target’s attention goes, with real scores from the trained mini model
scaled down

Query: the masked target (token #1, val32·churn). Both readings use the same raw scores q·k/√d_head (d_head = 16 here, 32 in the paper) . The block and head controls change which allowed keys win, never the 100%: the mask is the same in every block and every head . The literal ⊙ M reading is shown only to explain the correction; the code does not compute it.

The Python code never writes the −∞ itself. Each layer hands a precompiled block mask to FlexAttention, whose kernel sets the blocked scores to −∞ and skips tiles of the score matrix that are blocked entirely . The plain scaled-dot-product branch is never taken, because all four layers always receive a mask .
flex_attention applies the default scale 1/√E with E = d_head, and treats a 0 in the block mask as −∞ (spec §6.1).

The four attention masks of the live context

Rows are queries, columns are keys; a filled square means the query may attend to that key. The colored strips along both axes give each token’s table (key below), in emission order, so the blocks you see are rows and tables. Hover any square to compare that one pair in all four masks; click to pin the query (it carries over to the next chapters). The pinned query’s row is framed in violet.

Each mask has a shape you can read. The column mask is made of diagonal stripes. Rows of one table emit their cells in the same column order, so where such rows follow each other, the cells of one column recur at a fixed stride and their pairs line up parallel to the diagonal. Task rows have only two cells (timestamp and churn), so a run of task rows makes a small checkerboard. The feature mask has a small block on the diagonal for each row, because a row’s cells are emitted together and read each other. It also has a tall bar at keys 2–6: the cells of customers[35], which each of its 29 child rows in the context reads as a parent. The neighbor mask holds the same bar turned on its side, a band in query rows 2–6 where customers[35] reads its children. Step 6 shows that this is an exact transpose. The full mask is solid. The tick numbers on the axes are token positions. To read the blocks cell by cell, switch the figure to “First 20, labeled”.

query: the masked target · excerpt: 23 of 128 live tokens
“Full attention confers the expressive power of standard Transformers, complementing the relationally constrained layers above.”
Every non-padding token reads all 128 non-padding tokens, whatever their table, row or column. Padding tokens read nothing and are never read .
Expressivity: “Without full attention, information can only propagate one hop per layer, limiting expressivity to local message passing.”

sections.title: How much each mask lets through
blocks: The masks differ widely in density. In the live context of 128 positions, full attention allows every one of the 16,384 ordered pairs. The relational masks allow a small share of the 16,384: column 9.3%, feature 6.0%, neighbor 3.6%. The paper implements the layers “with sparse attention masks, and compiled to efficient FlashAttention-based kernels using FlexAttention” .
Allowed pairs per mask in the live context

Bars: the share of all 16,384 ordered pairs (S = 128) that each mask allows, on a fixed 0-100% axis; the count of allowed pairs follows each mask’s name. Keys per query are over the 128 non-padding queries. The neighbor mask is the only one with empty rows.

sections.title: Details that matter
blocks: The AND with “not padding”

When the sampler runs out of rows before L, the remaining positions are padding: node id −1, parent list [−1, −1, −1, −1, −1], every other field at its default . Left alone, those −1s would match each other. A real row with fewer than five parents has −1 slots in its parent list, so the test “key row ∈ query’s parents” would count every padding token as a parent. The code therefore ANDs every mask with pad[q,k]=¬ is_padding[q]∧¬ is_padding[k] . The full mask is nothing but pad.
Why the masks are ANDed with “not padding” (toy context of spec §6.3, 19 cells + 5 padding)

Left: the mask the code builds, (same_node | kv_in_f2p) & pad. Right: the same expression without & pad, evaluated on the raw ids (padding has node −1 and parents −1×5). The five padding tokens are the last rows and columns (gray strips). Without the AND, 24 of the 24 query rows change; the changed pairs are outlined in red. Where the labels do not fit (narrow screens), the axes show token positions instead.
With the AND in place, a padding query has an all-zero row in every mask and a padding key is never read. Padding inputs are the zero vector as well .
An empty row gives exactly zero

Column, feature and full rows always contain at least the query itself, so they are never empty. Only a neighbor row can be: when no row in the context points to the query’s row. In ShopDB that holds for every task row, every row of orders and reviews (no table has a foreign key to them) and any customer or product row whose child rows did not make it into the context. A softmax over nothing but −∞ would be 0/0. In the pinned PyTorch 2.6 FlexAttention kernel, a fully masked row outputs exactly 0, not NaN and not a uniform average . Because Wo has no bias, the residual update is 0 and the token passes through the sublayer unchanged. Our forward pass reproduces this, and you can check it live:
max |update| = 0 at 85 empty-neighbor tokens, all 4 blocks
other tokens: smallest max |update| 0.4022
scaled down
Neighbor is feature’s parent part, transposed

The feature mask has two parts: “same row” and “the key’s row is one of my parents”. The neighbor mask asks the reverse question: “the query’s row is one of the key’s parents” . Swapping the roles of query and key is a transpose, so neighbor is exactly the parent part of feature, flipped across the diagonal . Information that flows from parent to child in the feature layer flows from child to parent in the neighbor layer.
Neighbor is the feature mask’s parent part, transposed

Left: kv_in_f2p & pad, the part of the feature mask where the key’s row is a parent of the query’s row . Flipping it across the diagonal swaps query and key, which is exactly q_in_f2p & pad . First 40 tokens of the live context shown; the check below covers all 16,384 pairs.
The column test also checks the table

The column mask compares two ids, col_name_idxs and table_name_idxs, where the paper writes a single condition. The ids also decide which cells count as one column: the preprocessor interns the table name and the phrase “<col> of <table>” once per table, so Train, Val and Test task rows share both ids and the labels of every split meet in a single column group .
One mask for all heads
_make_block_mask calls create_block_mask with H=None, so a layer’s mask is broadcast over every head . Heads differ in which allowed keys they learn to weigh, never in which keys are allowed.
Built once, used by every block

Because the masks depend only on ids, the forward pass builds them once, before the first block, converts each to a FlexAttention block mask, and passes the same four block masks to all 12 blocks of the paper model (4 blocks here) . Inside a block the layers run in the order Column → Feature → Neighbor → Full, each picking its own mask .

blocks: All four kinds of attention layer in RT run the same computation, each with its own weights; what sets them apart is the mask that decides which token may read which. sections.title: Pick a sublayer and a query
blocks: Chapter 9 built four masks from the token ids. Each RT block uses them in four attention sublayers, always in the order column, feature, neighbor, full, and then applies a feed-forward sublayer . Every attention sublayer has its own RMSNorm and its own four projection matrices . The 4 blocks of the mini model therefore hold 16 different attention sublayers; the 12 blocks of the paper model hold 48 .

Choose one in the map. Each cell shows the length of the update, ‖Δx‖, that the sublayer adds to the query’s residual stream in the live forward pass. Then choose a query token: the masked target by default, or any other cell of the context. The choice is shared with the rest of this chapter and with chapters 7 to 9, so a token you inspected there is the query here.
The attention sublayers of the mini model, and the query token

For this query the Neighbor row of the map reads 0 in every block. No token in the context has the query’s row among its parents, so its row of the neighbor mask is empty, and an empty row gives an update of exactly zero . The other three layers always contain at least the query itself .

sections.title: Seven steps through one sublayer
blocks: Here is the sublayer as the code writes it. The block computes x+MHA(RMSNorm(x)), a pre-norm residual . Inside MHA, three linear maps without bias give queries, keys and values; these are split into heads; FlexAttention computes a masked softmax per head; and a fourth map Wo mixes the concatenated head outputs . For head j and query token q:
ℓ is the layer (column, feature, neighbor or full), Mℓ its mask, and Mask(a;M)=a where M[q,k]=1, −∞ otherwise.

The paper writes attention for a single head, with n queries and keys of dk numbers each and a divisor dk . With heads, dk is the width of one head (the dhead of other chapters): the code calls FlexAttention without a scale, and its default is 1/E, where E is the last dimension of each head’s query . That is 256 / 8 = 32 in the paper model and 64 / 4 = 16 here.

Two pieces of general Transformer background help to read the steps; they come from the original Transformer paper, not from RT . First, the three roles. A token’s query describes what it is looking for, each key describes what a token offers, and the score q⋅k measures how well the two match. The values are what the tokens hand over, averaged with the softmax weights. Second, the divisor. If the numbers in q and k were independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product would have variance dk. Wider heads would then give larger scores and push the softmax towards a single key, where its gradients are tiny. Dividing by dk brings the variance back to about 1.
Step through it below. Each step shows the live tensors on the left and the arithmetic, with this token’s numbers, on the right.

In step 3, head 1’s query uses all 64 numbers of h, but only its own 16 rows of Wq. The faded rows produce the other heads’ queries. Splitting the output this way is the reshape "b s (h d) -> b h s d" .

In step 5, switch the layer while the query is the masked target. The column mask keeps the cells of the label column, the feature mask keeps the target’s own row and its customer, the neighbor mask keeps nothing, and the full mask keeps every real token .
In step 6, the blocked keys do not get a small weight; they get exactly 0, because e−∞=0. The allowed weights alone sum to 1 .

When block 1’s column layer runs, each token is still its input embedding: a column-name term plus a value term, with no row, entity, time or position information . Two label cells with the same value are the same vector, so they get the same key and exactly the same weight, whoever they belong to . Only after the feature layer has written the customer into the target and into each task row can later blocks weigh their own customer’s labels differently.

In block 1, averaged over heads, the target gives 93.8% of its column-layer weight to its 12 self labels. sections.title: Implementation note: FlexAttention and a dense loop
blocks: The paper implements the relational layers “with sparse attention masks, and compiled to efficient FlashAttention-based kernels using FlexAttention” . The code compiles flex_attention once . In every forward pass, before the first block, it turns each dense boolean mask into a block mask , and every block reuses those four block masks . A block mask records which tiles of (query, key) pairs contain any allowed pair, so the kernel can skip the empty tiles .

This site runs in your browser without a GPU, so its engine loops over each query’s allowed keys in plain TypeScript. The arithmetic is the same masked softmax: scores scaled by 1/dhead, blocked keys excluded, weights normalized over the allowed keys . One case needs care. A query with no allowed key would divide 0 by 0. In the pinned PyTorch 2.6 kernel such a row outputs exactly 0, neither NaN nor a uniform average, and with a bias-free Wo the update is exactly 0 too . Our loop skips such rows by construction, which gives the same zeros. The checks below verify the output of our engine on the live forward pass:
340 query rows with no allowed key (all layers × 4 blocks): max |Δx| = 0 exactly
736,992 blocked (query, key) pairs × heads: largest weight = 0 exactly
6,832 rows of weights with at least one allowed key: max |Σp − 1| = 4.5e-8

Checked on the live forward pass of this context. 85 of the 128 real tokens have an empty neighbor row; column, feature and full rows of real tokens are never empty, since they always contain the query itself . Each empty row leaves its token unchanged, in every block . The sums miss 1 only by float32 rounding.

The remaining difference is precision. The paper runs the model in bfloat16 ; this site stores values in float32 and accumulates in float64, so its numbers are slightly more precise, not differently computed .

sections.title: The RT block and the residual stream
blocks: Attention is one sublayer. A block chains five of them: four attention layers (three relational, one full) and a gated feed-forward network, each adding its result to a running vector per token. This chapter assembles the block, stacks it, and follows the masked target through the whole stack with the live numbers of the trained mini model.

sections.title: One block, five sublayers
blocks: After the embedding of chapter 8, every token of the context is a vector of d = 64 numbers (256 in the paper). Inside the blocks the model never replaces that vector; it only adds to it. Each sublayer reads the token’s current vector, computes an update, and adds the update back: x←x+f(x) . The running vector is called the residual stream, and the identity path that carries it past every sublayer is the residual connection.

An RT block has five sublayers. Four are relational attentions, always in the order column, feature, neighbor, full; the fifth is a feed-forward network . Each has its own RMSNorm and its own weights: a block holds five RMSNorms, four separate attention modules and one feed-forward module .
One RT block, as the code runs it. Each line reads the x left by the line above.

Walk through a block below. The pulse travels with the followed token, the masked target by default; each box shows the length of the update it adds, ‖Δ‖, from the live forward pass. Click a box to inspect that sublayer.
An RT block, with the live numbers of one token

One box stays at zero for the target in every block: neighbor. The neighbor mask lets a row read only the rows that point to it, and no row has a foreign key to a task row: task tables have no primary key, so their rows are never parents , so the target has no key to read . A fully masked query returns exactly 0, and Wo has no bias, so the update is the zero vector . instead: its neighbor row has 76 keys, and its neighbor update is not zero.
Line 84 is the whole attention sublayer: normalize a copy, attend under this layer's mask, add the result. Line 85 does the same with the FFN.

sections.title: Pre-norm: where the norm sits
blocks: Every sublayer starts with an RMSNorm. It divides a vector by its root mean square and multiplies each dimension by a learned weight γi . Unlike LayerNorm it subtracts no mean and adds no bias.

The small constant ε = 2⁻⁷ is not a typo. The paper trained in bfloat16 , and the official code pins PyTorch 2.6.0, where nn.RMSNorm without an explicit ε uses the machine epsilon of the input type: 2⁻⁷ for bfloat16 . This site runs in float32 and keeps ε = 2⁻⁷ to match.
Algorithm 2 and the code disagree on placement

The paper’s Algorithm 2 normalizes the output of each sublayer before adding it. The code normalizes the input: the sublayer reads RMSNormℓ(x), and its raw output is added to the stream . This placement is called pre-norm.
X ← X + Norm(MHA(X; M))
The sublayer reads the raw stream and its output is normalized before the add.
x = x + attns[l](norms[l](x), …)
The sublayer reads a normalized copy; its raw output is added. The stream itself is never normalized inside the block.

Neither wiring rescales the stream itself inside a block: in both, x only ever receives additions. The original Transformer did rescale it, with x←LayerNorm(x+f(x)) . What the placement changes is what each sublayer reads and how large its update can be:
What a sublayer reads. In Algorithm 2 it reads the raw stream x. In the code it reads RMSNormℓ(x), whose length depends only on the direction of x and the weights γ, whatever the length of x.

How large an update can be. In Algorithm 2 every update passes through Norm, so its length is set the same way, whatever the sublayer computed. In the code the raw output is added, so the length of the update is free.

The chart shows both effects in the trained mini model, for the target. Its stream grows from ‖x‖ = 6.30 at the embedding to 14.79 after block 4 (blue); a sublayer that read the raw stream, as in Algorithm 2, would see vectors of these lengths. In the code every sublayer reads a copy whose length stays between 6.22 and 6.98 (orange). The updates it adds have lengths from 0.28 to 2.44, and exactly 0 where a sublayer has no key to read. The final RMSNorm, norm_out, is the only norm applied to the stream itself: it brings the length to 6.63 before the decoders read it .

sections.title: SwiGLU: the feed-forward sublayer
blocks: The fifth sublayer is a gated MLP. The paper says it uses “gated MLPs with SiLU activation, as found in the LLaMA architecture”, with a hidden dimension of 1024 . In the code it is three bias-free linear maps :

W1 and W3 map the normalized vector h from d = 64 to dff = 256 hidden units; W2 maps back to 64. The paper model uses 256 → 1024 → 256. In both, dff = 4d: RT does not use LLaMA’s ⅔ sizing of the hidden layer . The name SwiGLU joins Swish, another name for SiLU, with GLU, a gated linear unit : SiLU(W₁h) is the activation, and W₃h is a learned linear gate that multiplies it unit by unit.

The FFN works on each token by itself. It mixes the 64 dimensions of one token’s vector but never looks at another token. In an RT block, information moves between tokens only in the four attention sublayers.
SiLU, the gate, and the hidden units of a live token

blocks: 20 sublayers sit between the embedding and the decoders of the mini model (4 blocks × 5), and each one adds its update to the target’s stream. The grid measures every update; the matrix shows the vector itself after each stage, one row per stage, on a shared color scale. Pick another token to compare.

sections.title: How information can reach the target
blocks: In an attention sublayer, query q can receive from key k exactly when the mask allows the pair. The feed-forward sublayer works per token and moves nothing between tokens. Read in block order, the masks give a story for the target :
Column: the target reads every visible label of its column directly, its own customer’s past labels and other customers’ alike. It cannot yet tell which are which.
Feature: the target and every past task row read their parent customer’s cells, so each of them now carries information about which customer it concerns.
Neighbor: customer cells read their child rows, the labeled task rows and the orders and reviews rows alike. This is where per-customer aggregates can form, “analogously to message-passing in GNNs” .
Full: unrestricted mixing among all non-padding tokens.
Stacking blocks composes these hops: what a customer gathered in block 1’s neighbor layer reaches the target in block 2’s feature layer. Pick a source token below and trace it.
Route tracer: from any token to the masked target
Three routes on the live context, through the relational layers only (full attention switched off):
a past label of the same customer: #20 train258·churn → B1 column → target
an order of this customer: #7 o70·order_time → B1 neighbor → #2 c35·name → B2 feature → target
a cell of another customer: #111 c74·name → B1 column → #2 c35·name → B1 feature → target

The last route starts in a column layer: the customer’s own cells read the same column of every other customer in the context, and the target then reads its customer in a feature layer. Column attention links rows that no foreign key connects. With full attention every token reaches the target in block 1, since the full mask connects every pair of non-padding tokens. That is the point of the layer: it “enables long-range interactions in a fixed number of layers, independent of database or graph diameter” .

sections.title: Expressivity notes
blocks: If full attention can reach everything in one layer, why keep the three relational layers? The paper’s App. E discusses what each layer contributes to the expressive power of RT :
Column attention

“Removing column attention does not reduce expressivity, since global attention can emulate it. In particular, some global heads can learn to restrict attention to tokens from the same column by exploiting table and column name embeddings in their query–key construction.”
Not needed for expressivity, yet it is the layer with “the highest impact on zero-shot transfer” in the paper’s ablation (Table 5 below).
Feature attention
“Feature attention is the only mechanism that explicitly groups cells into rows.”

The paper adds that neighbor attention gives only partial row information (cells of one row see the same neighbors) and cannot uniquely tell rows apart, especially in tables without incoming foreign keys .
Neighbor attention

“Similar to column attention, neighbor attention is not strictly required for expressivity, as feature and global attention together can simulate its effect. Feature attention exposes F→P links, which global attention can then leverage to infer P→F relationships.”
In the masks, neighbor is exactly the transpose of the parent part of feature : every neighbor edge in the tracer above has a feature edge running the other way.
Full attention

“Without full attention, information can only propagate one hop per layer, limiting expressivity to local message passing. By contrast, full attention enables long-range interactions in a fixed number of layers, independent of database or graph diameter.”
Switch full attention off in the tracer to see the one-hop-per-layer limit on the live context.

sections.title: Decoders, loss and prediction
blocks: After the last block, every position holds a vector. This chapter turns the masked cell’s vector into an answer: four small linear heads, one per data type; a probability or a number in the column’s own units; the loss that training minimizes; and the two metrics the paper reports.
Why all four decoders run at every position, and which single output is read
How a logit becomes a probability, and a z-score becomes a number in the column’s units
The BCE and Huber losses with live numbers, and how a batch averages them
Why AUROC is computed on logits and R² in z-space, measured live on a whole split

sections.title: A final norm, then four decoders at every position
blocks: After the last block the forward pass applies one more RMSNorm, norm_out, to every position . Chapter 11 followed the vector up to this point. Next come the decoders, which the paper calls “cell decoders (also called prediction heads), one for each datatype” .

In the code the decoders are four nn.Linear layers in a dictionary, dec_dict. The number, datetime and boolean heads map the d-dimensional vector to a single value. The text head maps it to 384 values, the size of a MiniLM sentence embedding . All four have a bias.

The forward pass applies every head to the whole sequence, so each position, padding included, gets four outputs . Only one of these values is ever used: the output of the head that matches the masked cell’s type, at the masked position . In the paper’s words, “the decoder to select for final prediction depends on the task type, or equivalently on the datatype of the masked cell” . Step through it for the live context:
From the last block to four predictions

All values are the live forward pass of the mini model. The color of a cell is the sign and size of one coordinate (blue negative, red positive). Pick another position to see that the four heads produce outputs there too; only the masked cell’s own type is ever read.

The figure below zooms out to the whole context. Each column is one position and each row one decoder. Switch the view to see how the loss picks its single value: for each type i, the code builds sem_type_mask = (sem_types == i) & masks, so a position counts only if its token has that type and is the masked cell . Every other output is multiplied by zero.
Every position gets all four outputs (128 positions)

One column per position of the context, in token order. Each row is one decoder, colored by its output (blue negative, red positive, scaled per row). The text head’s 384 outputs per position are left out. The column with the dashed outline is the masked target. Hover or tap a column to read it; clicking also selects it in the figure above.
yhat = self.dec_dict[t](x) is a (B, S, D_t) tensor: all positions at once. A type with no masked cell in the batch still gets a zero-weight “touch”.
The text head is never trained

Text cells are never masked. The paper only masks “cells in boolean or numeric columns” , and the code refuses outright: raise ValueError("masking text not supported") . So no text output ever enters a loss, and the text head always falls in the “touch” branch: its gradient is exactly zero . One thing still moves it. The optimizer is a single AdamW parameter group with weight decay on every parameter , and you can see the trace of that in our checkpoint:
Checked on the loaded checkpoint (pretrain-churn)
no gradient ever reached the text head

Each of the 24,960 text-decoder parameters equals its initial value times 0.8467 (largest deviation 8e-6). A uniform shrink is exactly what weight decay alone does: AdamW multiplies every parameter by (1 − lr·wd) at each step, and with a zero gradient nothing else moves it. For comparison, the boolean head’s trained weights are no rescaling of their initial values at all: that head learned.
Reading the prediction

At evaluation time the code reads the boolean head for classification tasks and the number head for regression tasks, always at the positions flagged is_targets . Which tasks count as regression is decided by a hard-coded list of RelBench task names .

sections.title: Binary targets: from logit to probability
blocks: For a binary task the masked cell is a boolean, so the boolean head is read. Its output z^ is an unbounded real number, a logit. The paper-era code never turns it into a probability: the loss takes the logit directly , and so does the AUROC . A probability is still the natural number to show a person, and the authors’ later leaderboard script computes it with the sigmoid :

In the live context, the seed is customer 35 (Anna Müller). The task asks: “Will the customer place no order in the next 30 days? (churn = true means no order in (t, t+30d]).” The boolean head outputs z^=−0.198, so σ(z^)=0.451: the model gives a 45.1% chance that churn is true. The hidden answer is false.
From logit to probability

The curve is σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z)). The filled dot is the boolean head’s output at the masked cell; the slider moves a hollow dot to explore the curve. A logit of 0 is a probability of exactly 0.5.

The label is still inside the masked token: its boolean_values slot holds the true value, gated out of the input so the model cannot read it (chapter 7) . That stored value is a z-score, like every boolean (chapter 4). With a share μ of true values strictly between 0 and 1, true becomes (1−μ)/σ>0 and false becomes −μ/σ<0, so the sign alone recovers the class . That is why the paper writes the loss as BCE(1{r>0},r′) and why the evaluation converts labels with int(x > 0) .

sections.title: Regression targets: from z‑score to the column’s units
blocks: For a regression task the masked cell is a number, so the number head is read. Its output is a z-score: the prediction lives in the same normalized scale as the stored label . Each numeric column was z-scored with its own mean and sample standard deviation, and the Val and Test rows of a task table reuse the Train split’s statistics . Undoing the z-score gives the prediction in the column’s original units:
Like the sigmoid, this step is for display only. The paper-era code never leaves z-space; the authors’ later leaderboard script performs exactly this inversion with the Train statistics .

The global task is binary, so here is a local preview of product-sales: the seed is product 1 (Mechanical Keyboard), and the task asks “How many units of the product will be ordered in the next 30 days?” The number head outputs z^=+0.147. With the Train statistics μ = 4.380 and σ = 6.412, that is y^=5.32 sales; the hidden answer is 6.
From z-score to original units

One axis, two labelings: z above, sales below. Because ŷ = ẑ·σ + μ is a straight-line map, every point has both readings. Gray bars: the 321 Train labels whose μ and σ define the scale. The violet line is the number head’s output at the masked cell; the black line is the hidden label.

sections.title: The loss, with numbers
blocks: Training compares the read output with the hidden label. The paper: “we apply HuberLoss(r, r′) for regression and binary cross-entropy loss BCE(1{r > 0}, r′) for binary classification. The overall loss is the mean over all masked cells in the batch” . Here r is the cell’s normalized value, so both losses work on z-scores . The same objective is used in pretraining and in fine-tuning .
Binary cross-entropy with logits
F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits takes the logit and the 0/1 target and computes −log⁡σ(z^) for a positive and −log⁡(1−σ(z^)) for a negative, rearranged so that no exponential can overflow :
Binary cross-entropy with logits, at the masked cell

Each curve is the loss as a function of the logit for one value of the label. The dot is the live prediction on the curve of the actual label. A confident wrong logit costs about |z|; a confident right one costs almost nothing.
Huber loss

Number targets use F.huber_loss with its default δ = 1, on the residual between the predicted and the stored z-score . The paper does not say why it chose Huber; the curve shows what it does. Small errors are penalized like a squared error, large ones only linearly, so the gradient of a single cell never exceeds 1 in size: an unusual label, such as a product with a sudden burst of sales, pulls on the weights no harder than any other badly predicted cell.
Huber loss (δ = 1), at the masked cell

The solid curve is the Huber loss of the residual d = ẑ − z, both in z-space. Inside the shaded band (|d| < 1) it equals ½d², the dashed parabola; outside it grows only linearly, |d| − ½, so its slope never exceeds 1.
The mean over the masked cells of a batch
The code adds up the loss of every masked cell, type by type, and divides by the number of masked cells, loss_out / masks.sum() :

Each context has exactly one masked cell, so this is the plain mean over the contexts of the batch, 32 per GPU in the paper; DDP then averages the gradients over 8 GPUs, which gives the mean over 256 . There is no weight per task, per type or per class, and no label smoothing . Pretraining shuffles the items of all its tasks into one list, so a batch can mix binary and regression cells :
A mini batch of 8 training contexts: one masked cell each

4 Train rows of customer-churn and 4 of product-sales, each with its own sampled context (epoch 0), run through one model (checkpoint pretrain-churn). Bars are the per-cell losses; the line is their mean, the number the optimizer minimizes. The batch is an illustration: these exact steps were never taken in training.

sections.title: Metrics: AUROC on logits, R² in z‑space
blocks: The paper scores binary tasks with AUROC and regression tasks with R² . The evaluation loop collects the read output and the stored label of every evaluated seed, then calls scikit-learn once per task and split . Each seed gets one context and one forward pass, with no averaging over several contexts : “a single forward pass” .
AUROC

AUROC is the area under the ROC curve. It also has a direct reading: pick one seed whose label is 1 and one whose label is 0 at random; AUROC is the probability that the first gets the higher score, with ties counting half. Only the order of the scores matters. The sigmoid never changes the order of two logits, so AUROC on logits equals AUROC on probabilities, and the code can skip the sigmoid . The figure evaluates every seed of the split in your browser.
AUROC on the logits: how well the scores rank the two classes

Left: the ROC curve, true-positive rate against false-positive rate as the threshold sweeps down the logits. Right: every seed’s logit, split by its label. The violet threshold line and the violet dot on the curve move together. AUROC is the shaded area under the curve.
R² compares the squared errors of the predictions with those of the simplest possible predictor, the mean label yˉ of the evaluated seeds:

Predicting yˉ for every seed scores exactly 0, which is why the paper’s Table 2 notes “Global mean baseline is 0.0” . A negative R² is worse than that baseline. The code computes R² on z-scores. Converting labels and predictions to original units multiplies both sums by σ², and the ratio does not change .
R² in z-space: how much of the labels’ spread the predictions explain

Each dot is one seed: its label against the number head’s prediction. Dots on the diagonal are perfect. The dashed line predicts the mean label ȳ for everyone, which scores R² = 0 by definition. Switching to original units rescales both axes by σ and leaves R² unchanged.

sections.title: One decoder per type, shared by everything
blocks: There is one number head and one boolean head for the whole model, not one per column, table or database . The same handful of weights predicts the sales of a product, the rating of a review and, in the pretraining databases, the grade of a submission or the points of a driver. Its output is read in the target column’s own z-space, as a number of standard deviations above that column’s mean . The head never learns which column it is predicting; that information reaches it only through x^, which carries the column-name embedding of the masked token (chapter 8).
One output value, read in each target column’s own scale

Every target of every task in the four databases. The same decoder serves all the rows of one type: its output is a z-score of the target column (number rows) or a logit (boolean rows). Statistics are recomputed live from each database’s preprocessing.

This sharing is what lets a pretrained model answer for a column it has never seen. Our pretrained heads learned from the targets of SchoolDB, RacingDB and ForumDB, and are read on ShopDB without any weight update . Per-column z-scoring is what lets one output scale serve them all: over the rows that define its statistics, every regression target has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

sections.title: Pretraining, zero-shot, fine-tuning
blocks: Every chapter so far ran the model with trained weights. This one shows where they come from: one hidden cell per context, a database held out, a one-cycle learning-rate schedule, a checkpoint chosen per task, then fine-tuning. All of it from this site’s real training run, next to the paper’s recipe.
What RT is trained to do: recover one masked cell per context, with one loss for pretraining and fine-tuning
What leave-one-database-out means, and why choosing a checkpoint on the target’s validation labels still counts as zero-shot
How the learning rate and Adam’s β1 move during training, and where the code differs from the paper’s description
What our miniature run achieved on ShopDB, before and after fine-tuning, and what it cannot tell you

sections.title: One masked cell per context
blocks: Pretraining gives RT the same exercise it will face at test time. Take a seed row of some task, sample its context window (chapter 6), hide one cell, and ask the model to recover it. The hidden cell is always the seed’s own target: the label of a forecasting task row, or the target column of a row for an autocomplete task. There is exactly one masked cell per context, and every other cell, past labels included, stays visible .
masks marks the cells the loss is computed on; it is set to is_target, so one cell per sequence.

The model predicts that cell with the decoder of its type and is scored with the loss of that type: binary cross-entropy against 1{y > 0} for a boolean, the Huber loss with δ = 1 for a number, both on z-scored values. “The overall loss is the mean over all masked cells in the batch”, and “this formulation is used in both pretraining and fine-tuning” . Fine-tuning changes the data, never the objective. Chapter 12 works through both losses with live numbers.

Which seeds? Pretraining builds one dataset over every training task of every pretraining database, all on their training split . A forecasting task contributes the rows of its Train split; an autocomplete task contributes every row of its table that has the target cell . These items go into a single list with no balancing, so a task’s share of the training signal is its share of the rows . Step through how one batch of our run comes together:

Seed lists and contexts are computed live by this site’s engine, the same code that exported our training data. Tasks enter in proportion to their number of seed rows: autocomplete tasks, which use every row of a table, dominate .

In our run the four autocomplete tasks supply 78% of all items, because they use every row of their table (submissions, votes, results), while a forecasting task has one row per entity and timestamp. A batch therefore mixes databases, tasks, booleans and numbers, and every optimizer step averages its gradient over all of them. In the running example the masked cell is customer 35’s label in customer-churn. ShopDB never appears in pretraining: for it, the same exercise is the test.
The code behind the figure
From the task list to the batch loss, in the order the figure steps through. Pick an excerpt.
Every task tuple gets the split "train"; for autocomplete tasks data.py then resolves it to the whole DB table.

sections.title: Leave one database out
blocks: Zero-shot means “predicting new targets on a new RDB with a new schema, without weight updates. Information about the new RDB is available only at inference time, solely through the context window” . To test this honestly, the target database must stay out of pretraining. So the paper pretrains “separately for each target dataset on all tasks from all other datasets” : leave-one-database-out. RelBench has seven databases. rel-event is in every pretraining mix but never evaluated, “as it has been found to have temporal leakage issues” .
Counts are computed live by the engine. Forecast tasks contribute their Train split; autocomplete tasks every row of their table . ShopDB’s tables, column names and rows never reach the optimizer.
The pretraining script expresses the whole protocol as two list filters: train on every task whose database is not rel-amazon, evaluate rel-amazon’s forecasting tasks, on val and test .
That leaves 30 training tasks for rel-amazon; across targets, 29 to 33 (spec §9.1).

We do the same with four synthetic databases: SchoolDB, RacingDB and ForumDB for pretraining, ShopDB held out. ShopDB’s tables, column names and rows never reach the optimizer. The one thing it shares with the pretraining data is the frozen text encoder, which embeds every column phrase and string of every database the same way (chapter 5).

Why should anything transfer? The paper expects it “as databases share structural commonalities, e.g., dimension tables, fact tables, hubs and tripartite structures, as well as semantic similarities” . It later finds the main driver is the target entity’s own past labels . Our generators give every pretraining forecast task that property: an entity’s label in one window correlates with its label in the next, with lag-1 correlations from 0.42 to 0.73 (results.json). A model that learns to read an entity’s history in SchoolDB can use the same skill on a ShopDB customer.

sections.title: The learning-rate schedule
blocks: The optimizer is AdamW with weight decay 0.1 and a peak learning rate of 10⁻³ . The schedule is PyTorch’s OneCycleLR: the learning rate η climbs linearly for the first 20% of the steps, then falls linearly for the rest . The code passes only the peak, the number of steps, the 20% and the word “linear”, so PyTorch’s defaults decide the rest. The climb starts at the peak divided by 25, 4·10⁻⁵; the fall ends at that value divided by 10⁴, 4·10⁻⁹; and with cycle_momentum on, Adam’s β1 moves the opposite way, from 0.95 down to 0.85 at the peak and back .
Both runs use the same scheduler with T = total steps, so their shapes match and only the step axis stretches. The paper’s curve is sampled every 250 steps; ours is logged at every update .

β1 is Adam’s momentum: how much of the previous update direction each step keeps. The paper does not explain its choice of schedule. The one-cycle policy comes from Smith and Topin, who warm up to a large learning rate and then anneal it for most of training , and Smith recommends lowering momentum while the learning rate is high . The coded betas = (0.9, 0.999) therefore never apply as written: the scheduler overwrites β1 at every step.
net.parameters() is a single group, so weight decay also applies to RMSNorm gains, biases and the mask vectors (spec §9.2).

sections.title: Our training run
blocks: This is the run behind every trained number on the site. It follows the paper’s recipe at a smaller scale: the same objective, optimizer, schedule and clipping, with 4,001 steps of 32 contexts instead of 50,001 steps of 256. Each step is the code’s train step: forward pass and loss, clear the old gradients, backward pass, measure the global gradient norm, clip it to 1.0, one AdamW update, one scheduler step .

Every step is one batch of 32 contexts from all three pretraining databases, so the loss jumps with the batch’s mix of tasks; the moving average shows the trend. The norm is measured before clipping, as the code logs it .

The loss falls from about 0.45 in the first 100 steps to about 0.31 over the last 200, and it stays noisy from step to step because each batch draws a different mix of tasks. It never approaches zero: a context holds only so much information about its hidden cell, and our generators draw every label from a random process.

sections.title: Choosing the checkpoint, task by task
blocks: While it pretrains, the code evaluates the held-out database at step 0, every eval_freq steps and at every power of two. For each target task it keeps the checkpoint with the best validation metric and, at that moment, records the test metric of the same step . The numbers the run prints at the end, and the paper reports, are those recorded test metrics . Selection is per task because the authors “found significant overfitting during pretraining due to limited pretraining tasks” .
Both metrics are higher-is-better (AUROC on logits, R² in z-space), so one comparison serves both task types.
53 evaluations at step 0, every 100 steps and at every power of two, before that step’s update . The rule is a strict “greater than”, starting from −∞ .

In our run, customer-churn keeps step 2,500 and product-sales keeps step 600. One pretraining run, one checkpoint per task: that is why the site ships a pretrain-churn and a pretrain-sales file (plus pretrain-rating and pretrain-verified for the two review tasks, and pretrain-final, the last step), and why the global “auto” checkpoint depends on the task. Notice also how much the validation curve moves between neighboring evaluations: up to 3.4 AUROC points for customer-churn, on 71 validation seeds. With so few seeds, which step wins is partly chance. At the chosen step the test AUROC is 77.9; at the last step it would have been 79.1.

sections.title: Results on ShopDB
blocks: Now the numbers. For each ShopDB forecasting task the figure places five models on one axis: an untrained network, the EntityMean baseline, RT zero-shot, and RT fine-tuned on ShopDB’s Train split from a random init and from the pretrained checkpoint. Churn is scored by AUROC and sales by R², both in percent as in the paper’s tables.
Every RT number is the test metric recorded at the step with the best validation metric, as in the paper . EntityMean predicts the mean of the entity’s past labels, falling back to the Train mean .
What the run shows:
Customer churn. Zero-shot RT reaches a test AUROC of 77.9, above EntityMean (76.9) and above the untrained network (75.5). On validation the order is the same: 74.9 vs 71.3 vs 69.0.

Product sales. Zero-shot RT reaches a test R² of 58.5, below EntityMean (74.8). Pretraining alone lifts it from −27.6 for the untrained network, without a single gradient from ShopDB. EntityMean is a strong baseline for counts that persist; the paper sees the same on two of its eight regression tasks, where EntityMean beats RT (item-ltv 54.2 vs 32.5, post-votes 43.7 vs 33.9) .

Fine-tuning. Selected on validation, fine-tuning from the pretrained checkpoint gives a test 71.7 on churn and 67.9 on sales; from random init, 66.3 and 49.1. Step 7 shows the curves behind these numbers.
And what it does not show:

Small test sets. 74 test seeds for churn and 30 for sales. Differences of a few points are within noise. The next figure makes this concrete: untrained networks, which have learned nothing, already spread from 29.6 to 75.5 test AUROC on churn, depending only on their random seed.

Simple synthetic data. Three small pretraining databases and ten tasks, against the paper’s six real databases and about thirty tasks. Our numbers show that the mechanism runs end to end; they do not show how RT compares with anything.

Dots: PyTorch-default initializations after torch.manual_seed(s), s = 0…6. The filled dot, s = 0, is the starting point of our pretraining run. Vertical lines: the pretrained zero-shot model (blue) and EntityMean (gray) on the same split.

Why is an untrained network not at 50? Its output is a fixed but random function of the context, and the context carries information about the label, past labels included. On 74 test seeds, some random functions happen to rank churners above loyal customers and others below. PyTorch draws every initial weight and bias from an interval symmetric around zero , so a network and its twin with the boolean decoder’s weights and bias negated are equally likely. The twin outputs the opposite logit for every seed and ranks every pair the other way round (AUROC 100 − x), so the expected AUROC over initializations is 50. Any single network is one draw from a wide distribution.
The metrics average over every seed. To see what training changes for one prediction, here is the running example’s context passed through the three checkpoints of its task:

The tokens and masks are identical in the three cards; the decoder output at the masked cell changes only because the weights do. One context is an anecdote: the metrics above average over every seed of the split.

Every number in this section can be recomputed in your browser: the panel below rebuilds each seed’s context with the engine, runs the exported weights, and computes the metric as the code does, AUROC on raw logits and R² in z-space .

L = 128, w = 16 and the evaluation RNG seed 0, as in training, whatever the global simulation settings say . The browser runs the TypeScript forward pass, which agrees with PyTorch to at most 2.6×10⁻⁶ at every activation of the verified contexts (chapter 16), so the metrics agree to the shown digits unless two seeds’ predictions are nearly tied.

sections.title: Fine-tuning: pretrained vs random init
blocks: Fine-tuning trains on the target task itself: its Train split only, with the same objective, a constant learning rate of 10⁻⁴ and no weight decay . Checkpoints store only the model weights, so a new AdamW starts with empty moments and no warmup . The paper compares starting from the pretrained checkpoint with starting from random weights, which it calls untrained RT, and plots both against fine-tuning steps on a log axis .

Same axes as the paper’s Figure 3: fine-tuning steps + 1 on a log scale, the first point being step 0 . Rings mark the step each run would keep (best val). Evaluations at step 0, at every power of two and every 64 steps.

A head start. The pretrained run starts where zero-shot ends (sales test R² 58.5), the random init at −27.6. The paper’s Figure 3 shows the same kind of gap: its pretrained curves start at the labeled zero-shot points, 70.8 AUROC and 29.0 R², and the untrained ones start below the bottom of its axes .

A dip first. In its first updates the pretrained sales run drops from 58.5 to 51.6 (step 1) before it climbs. The paper sees “a small dip in performance in the very early steps, which we conjecture might be due to the model transitioning from a zero-shot, in-context-labels- and semantics-driven regime to a data-driven prediction regime” .

Overfitting. ShopDB’s churn Train split has 601 rows, and 1,025 steps of 32 contexts revisit each about 55 times. Switch to “training loss”: it keeps falling, while the test AUROC peaks at 78.2 (step 8) and ends at 58.6. Validation selection keeps step 192, with test 71.7, below zero-shot (77.9). The paper’s Figure 3 averages only tasks “which do not show overfitting” ; its per-task curves for the small rel-f1 tasks bend down the same way .

Paper rows: a few of the 18 tasks of Table 12 (p.23). On rel-trial study-outcome no label reaches the context, and zero-shot AUROC there is 51.8, close to random (Table 1). sections.title: Names carry meaning
blocks: Every token’s input contains the embedding of its column phrase, such as “churn of customer-churn” or “price of products”, from the frozen text encoder . On an unseen database these names are the model’s only clue to what a column means. Shuffling them asks how much it relies on that clue.

In the paper, shuffling column and table names lowers the mean zero-shot AUROC from 70.1 to 69.5 and the mean R² from 22.8 to 20.5: “wrong names lead to consistent degradation” . After fine-tuning the effect disappears (77.5 vs 77.2 AUROC).

Our version permutes the 384-dimensional phrase embeddings among the columns present in the context, in one random cycle, so every column receives another column’s name. The phrase includes the table name, so table names move with it. The masks are untouched, because the sampler stores a column’s id (read by the masks) and its phrase embedding (read by the input layer) in two separate arrays:
col_name_idxs feeds the column mask (model.py:181-183); col_name_values feeds the input embedding (model.py:211). The shuffle permutes only the second.
Every non-padding token, the masked cell included, gets RMSNorm(W·c + b) of its column phrase c. Shuffling swaps c between columns.

sections.title: A shorter or a longer context
blocks: Attention cost grows with the context length L. Figure 4 of the paper evaluates a model pretrained at L = 1024 with shorter contexts at inference: L = 256, 512, 768, 1024 . Its summary: “RT’s performance degrades gracefully, showing a drop of only 4% absolute AUROC and 7% absolute R² with 25% lower time and 20% lower memory.” .

The sampler’s random generator is seeded with the epoch, the seed row and a fixed offset, never with L , and L is only read by the stop test . So with the same seed row a shorter context is exactly the first L cells of a longer one. We checked this for all 1,733 ShopDB seeds of every task and split, at every L of the sweep against L = 256. sections.title: What the paper concluded
blocks: The authors rank the components that enable zero-shot transfer, “in order of importance” :
Time-series forecasting from past task rows for the target entity.
Column attention with the help of Relational Attention to generalize to new column distributions.

Schema semantics from table and column names.
In-context learning from task rows for other entities.

sections.title: Zero-shot classification
blocks: Zero-shot has a precise meaning in the paper: “predicting new targets on a new RDB with a new schema, without weight updates. Information about the new RDB is available only at inference time, solely through the context window” . In every column of Table 1 the target task is unseen during pretraining . The columns differ in what else the model has seen:
No: the target database was held out entirely. RT is pretrained on the six other RelBench databases (leave-one-database-out) .
Yes: RT then continued pretraining on the target database’s other tasks; the target task stays unseen .
Maybe: the Gemma3 LLMs, whose pretraining data “is unknown, but likely includes similar public datasets” . They read the same context subgraph serialized as JSON, plus dataset and task descriptions .

The non-neural EntityMean baseline predicts the mean of the target entity’s past labels . It is a strong baseline because those past labels are informative, a point the ablations below return to. Random guessing scores 50.
Mean zero-shot AUROC over 10 binary tasks
Table 1 · p.8

Each stem starts at the random baseline (AUROC 50) and ends at the method’s mean, as printed. Circles: the target database was never seen (“No”). Squares: continued pretraining on the target database’s other tasks (“Yes”). The target task itself is unseen in every column . Hover a row for what the method is.

Among the methods that never saw the target database, RT (No) has the highest mean, 69.7, ahead of EntityMean (66.7) and Griffin (64.0); the largest LLM reaches 64.6. The paper reports that RT “attains the best average AUROC and is the only method to consistently beat the entity mean baseline” . Task by task the picture is more mixed: EntityMean is higher on 4 of 10 tasks (EntityMean vs RT: amazon · item-churn, 73.0 vs 70.9; amazon · user-churn, 64.4 vs 64.0; hm · user-churn, 64.4 vs 62.8; stack · user-engage, 83.5 vs 75.7). sections.title: Learning efficiency
blocks: Zero-shot is only the first point of a longer curve. “The key promise of pretraining is efficient adaptation to new datasets and tasks” . On each unseen task the paper fine-tunes for 33k steps at a constant learning rate of 10⁻⁴ with no weight decay , and compares pretrained RT with untrained RT, an untrained RDL-GNN and Griffin .

sections.title: What the context contributes
blocks: To find out where zero-shot transfer comes from, the authors keep the pretrained checkpoints and change the context: they shuffle the column and table names, remove the target entity’s past task rows (self labels), or remove other entities’ task rows (other labels) . They repeat each ablation with fine-tuning on the modified contexts . The matrix holds Table 4’s means; click any cell to see it task by task.
Context ablations
Tables 4 and 11 · p.9, p.22

Self labels dominate. Without them, zero-shot AUROC falls from 70.1 to 53.8 and R² from 22.8 to −5.5, worse than predicting the mean. “Zero-shot transfer is driven primarily by the model’s ability to leverage past labels of the target entity” . Yet RT is not just averaging them: it beats EntityMean, which does exactly that . After fine-tuning, the ablations barely move the means, except that removing self labels still costs regression 6.5 points of R² .
If self labels drive transfer, tasks whose contexts hold none should not suffer when they are removed. The paper’s own label counts (Table 12) let us check this.
Where self labels exist, removing them hurts
Tables 12 and 11 · p.23, p.22

Each point is one task. Horizontal: how many past labels of the target entity the sampler put into a 1024-cell context, on average (the standard deviations are large; see the tooltip or the table) . Vertical: the change in zero-shot AUROC when those self labels are removed . Both tables date from the paper’s first version . The two tasks whose contexts hold no self labels at all, rel-trial study-outcome and study-adverse, do not change when they are removed.

The paper’s Figure 5 asks the follow-up question: without self labels, does pretraining still help fine-tuning? It plots fine-tuning curves of pretrained RT with and without self labels and of untrained RT without them, and shades the gap between the two curves without self labels as positive transfer . Their reading is that RT does learn other transferable patterns, “but self labels do constitute the dominant share of transfer from pretraining even during initial steps of fine-tuning” .

Self labels exist because task-table prompting puts the entity’s past task rows within reach of the sampler, and column attention lets the masked cell read their labels. Here is Table 12’s count for the live task, followed by our miniature’s answer to “what if there were no labels at all?”

sections.title: What the architecture contributes
blocks: The architecture ablations retrain RT with one of the four attention layer types removed from every block, adding blocks to keep the parameter count constant . How many blocks were added is not reported, and none of the ablation code is released .
Attention-layer ablations
Tables 5 and 13 · p.10, p.23

Column attention matters most for zero-shot transfer: without it, zero-shot R² drops from 22.8 to 11.9 . The paper reads the fine-tuned columns as “the impact is less pronounced, and the impact of feature and neighbor attention is more significant”, and adds that “removing full attention has the least impact in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings, even significantly improving the results on some tasks” . The first part holds for AUROC; on fine-tuned R², removing column attention still costs the most . For classification, the differences are minor .
Does the order of the layers matter?

The released block runs column → feature → neighbor → full (“CFN”); the ICLR-submission code ran feature → neighbor → column → full (“FNC”; Table 15’s codes leave the final full layer implicit) . Table 15 trains every order, plus a variant that runs the three relational layers in parallel and sums their outputs . Zero-shot means span only 69.3–70.6 AUROC and 22.1–23.6 R²: “the specific order of relational attention layers is not critical to performance” .

Masking more than one cell

The released sampler masks exactly one cell per context, the seed’s target . Table 14 pretrains with extra cells masked with probability P(mask), each contributing to the loss . More masking lowers zero-shot R² (22.8 → 16.9 → 15.3) but raises fine-tuned R² (33.2 → 35.6 at 0.2, 34.4 at 0.4). The “no pretraining” column fine-tunes from random initialization.

sections.title: Limitations
blocks: The authors name three limitations and one direction for future work.
No recommendation or link prediction
“Limitations of RT include inability to handle recommendation or link prediction tasks.”
RT casts every task as predicting one masked cell . Recommendation and link prediction ask which rows should be linked; the paper names supporting them as future work.
Ch. 3: tasks as masked cells →
Key column names are ignored
“it does not incorporate the names of primary-key and foreign-key columns, which often carry useful semantics.”
PK and FK columns never become tokens; they only define rows and links, so a name like customer_id is never embedded .
Ch. 2: feature vs key columns →
Two foreign keys to one table look alike
“RT also does not disambiguate between different foreign key columns.”
A row’s parents are stored as a bare list of row ids. Nothing records which key column each id came from. Try it below.
Ch. 9: the feature and neighbor masks →
Simple cell encoders
“more advanced cell encoders can be explored, including graph positional encodings, to enhance performance for supervised fine-tuning settings in large-data regimes.”
Today each value enters through one linear layer and an RMSNorm per type , and there are no positional encodings .
Ch. 8: the token embedding →
The paper’s example, made concrete: who bought, who sold?

An illustration of the example on p.10 (row ids are made up). The preprocessor turns each foreign-key value into a parent row id and pushes it onto f2p_nbr_idxs; the column name is dropped . The feature and neighbor masks then only ask whether a row is in that list . Swapping the two values reorders the list, and nothing else the masks see.
ptable_offset is the parent table’s first global node index (spec §1.5).
.any(-1) reduces over the five parent slots: which slot matched is never used.
Scope of the evaluation

All results cover RelBench’s forecasting tasks. Autocomplete tasks are used in pretraining but are not part of the standard benchmark, and rel-event is skipped “as it has been found to have temporal leakage issues” . Each run pretrains on six databases .
