sections.title: Glossary
blocks: Every term defined in this course, with where it is documented. Hover a dotted term anywhere on the site for the same definition.
AUROC
Area under the ROC curve, computed on raw logits (identical to using sigmoid probabilities). Metric for binary tasks.
Autocomplete task
Predict a masked cell of an existing DB column. The seed is a DB row, no task rows enter the context, and leakage columns are dropped on the fly.
See also:
BCE with logits
Loss for boolean targets against 1{z > 0}, where z is the z-scored label (z > 0 exactly when the label is true).
BFS width bound (w)
At most w DB children are kept per visited row, sampled uniformly after the temporal filter. Task-table children are never subsampled. Paper scripts use w = 256.
Cell token
One non-missing feature cell, represented by its value, its column name and its table name. RT’s sequence is made of these, not of rows.
Column attention
A token attends to every token of the same column of the same table. The masked label sees every visible label cell of its task.
Column phrase
The string “<column> of <table>”, e.g. “age of customers”. Its MiniLM embedding is how a token learns which column and table it belongs to.
See also:
Context window (L)
The L cell tokens gathered around the seed by the sampler (paper L = 1024). Sampling stops at exactly L tokens, even mid-row, or pads when the frontier empties.
Depth label
The hop count carried by a frontier entry (+1 per F→P or P→F hop). The next P→F row is drawn uniformly from the lowest non-empty depth bucket.
EntityMean
Baseline: the mean of the target entity’s past labels, falling back to the global training mean of the target column.
F→P link
From a row that holds a foreign key to the row it references (its parent). The sampler always follows these first, without time filtering or subsampling.
Feature attention
A token attends to its own row and to its parent rows (the rows its FKs point to): row-wise attention after joining each table with its parents.
Feature column
Any column that is not a primary or foreign key. Its non-missing cells are what RT turns into tokens (number, text, datetime or boolean).
See also: ,
Forecasting task
Predict an entity’s label over a future window (t, t+Δ] from data up to t, e.g. whether a customer places no order in the next 30 days.
Foreign key (FK)

A column holding the row position of a parent row in another table. It produces no token, only links: the parent id joins the child’s f2p_nbr_idxs and the parent gets a P→F edge back. At most 5 non-null FKs per row.
See also: ,
Full attention
Every non-padding token attends to every other one. The paper also calls it “global” attention.
Global node index

One integer id per row across every table of a database, task-table splits included: offset of the table file plus the row position. DB tables come first (sorted by name), then task splits test < train < val.
Huber loss
Loss for number (and datetime) targets in z-space with δ = 1: 0.5d² if |d| < 1, else |d| − 0.5.
In-context label
A visible label cell in the context: another row of the same task table (the target entity’s past rows or other entities’ rows), or for autocomplete, other rows of the target column.
See also: ,
Leakage columns
Per-task columns_to_drop (autocomplete only). Their cells are skipped for the seed row and for rows whose timestamp equals the seed’s.
Leave-one-DB-out pretraining
Pretrain on all tasks of every other database, then evaluate zero-shot on the held-out one. Best validation checkpoint kept per target task.
Mask vector mₜ
A learned vector per sem type, added raw (not normalized) in place of the value term of the masked cell.
Masked target cell
The single masked token of a context: the seed row’s label cell. It keeps its column name and type, but its value embedding is replaced by the learned mask vector.
See also:
Neighbor attention
A parent’s tokens attend to the tokens of its child rows in the context, like GNN message passing. A row with no children in the context gets a zero update.
P→F link
The reverse of an F→P link: from a parent row to each child row that references it. A row can have unboundedly many children, so the sampler time-filters and width-bounds them.
Padding token
A filler position when fewer than L cells were sampled: node −1, every field at its default, is_padding = true. Its input is the zero vector and every mask excludes it.
Permutation equivariance

Reordering the input tokens reorders the outputs in the same way: each token’s final hidden state moves with it and does not change. RT has it because its inputs depend only on each token’s own fields and its masks only on ids.
See also:
Permutation invariance
RT has no positional encodings: shuffling the tokens permutes the outputs identically, so the prediction at the target does not change.
See also:
Pre-norm residual
Each sublayer computes x + f(RMSNorm(x)). The code is pre-norm, although the paper’s Algorithm 2 writes the norm after the sublayer.
Primary key (PK)
The column that identifies a row. It produces no token and no edge; in RelBench-style data its value equals the row position 0..n−1.
Coefficient of determination, computed in z-space (equal to raw-unit R²). 0 is the global-mean baseline. Metric for regression tasks.
Relational attention
Multi-head attention restricted by a boolean mask built from table, column and row ids. RT uses four kinds per block: column, feature, neighbor and full.
Relational database
A set of tables whose rows are linked through primary and foreign keys. RT reads it as one graph of rows plus a pool of feature cells.
RMSNorm
y = x / √(mean(x²) + ε) · γ. RT applies one before every sublayer, after every input projection and once at the end; ε = 2⁻⁷ in the paper’s bf16 environment.
Row timestamp
Whole seconds of the time column, set only for rows that have a time column, a non-null time value and at least one non-null FK. Rows without one always pass the temporal filter.
Same-horizon rows
Other entities’ task rows with the same timestamp as the seed. The released sampler keeps them (filter is child_ts > seed_ts), so their labels are visible.
Seed row
The row whose target cell is predicted. Its cells come first in the context, and the BFS starts from it.
Self label
An in-context label of the target entity itself (its past task rows). Removing them is the largest zero-shot ablation in the paper.
Semantic type
Number (0), Text (1), DateTime (2) or Boolean (3), decided only by the physical dtype: integers and floats are numbers, strings are text. Each type has its own encoder, decoder and mask vector.
SwiGLU feed-forward
FFN(h) = W₂(SiLU(W₁h) ⊙ W₃h) with no biases, 4× hidden width (256 → 1024 → 256 in the paper).
Task table
A table holding the prediction task: a timestamp, one FK to the entity and the label. It is attached to the database as an ordinary table, with Train, Val and Test splits.
See also:
Task-table prompting
Specifying the task by attaching its task table to the database. Its rows are the seeds, and past rows of the same task, reached through the entity, carry visible labels.
Temporal filter
A P→F child is skipped only if both timestamps exist and the child’s is later than the seed’s. Equal timestamps pass; parents are never filtered.
Text encoder
The frozen sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L12-v2 model (384-d, mean pooled, unit norm). It embeds column phrases, table names and text cell values once, ahead of time.
Time column
The one datetime column a table may declare. It is an ordinary datetime token, and also the source of the row’s integer timestamp used by the sampler.
See also:
z-score normalization

Numbers and booleans are standardized per column, (v − μ)/σ with the sample std; datetimes use one global mean and population std per database. Task-label stats come from the Train split; DB-table stats from all rows.
Zero-shot
Predicting on a database (or task) never trained on, with no weight updates; the new data enters only through the context window. Checkpoints are still selected on the target task’s validation split.

sections.title: Two halves: built once, run on every change
blocks: The site has two halves. The offline half ran once, on a CPU. It generated four small databases, embedded every string with the frozen text encoder, trained the model and checked it. Its results are plain files in public/data/.

The online half runs in your browser whenever you change a setting. It regenerates the database, preprocesses it, samples a context window and runs the forward pass with the shipped weights and embeddings. No server computes anything.

One decision holds the two halves together: the same TypeScript preprocessing and sampler produce the training contexts offline and the live context here. The model was trained on exactly the kind of token sequence the chapters display, and there is no second sampler that could drift from the first. Click a stage, or press play, to see what it does and its numbers right now.
The pipeline, stage by stage

Cards marked “shared code” run the same TypeScript in both halves. The dashed band holds the committed files that carry the offline results to your browser. Every number in the panel is live: read from those files or computed on this page.

sections.title: Three implementations of one function
blocks: A browser cannot run the official model: it is PyTorch code that needs FlexAttention, a compiled attention kernel . So the model exists here three times, and the checks connect them in a chain.
The official class RelationalTransformer from rt/model.py at the paper-era commit, run unmodified apart from one pinned setting (RMSNorm ε, below). It only ever serves as the reference.
A PyTorch port with the same module and parameter names, so a checkpoint loads into either class. It swaps FlexAttention for dense masked attention and trains the model.
The browser engine, plain TypeScript, which runs every forward pass on this site.
What was compared with what
Bounds from public/data/verification.json, written by the verification step of the pipeline.

Why are the differences not exactly zero? Every value is a float32, which keeps about seven significant digits. The implementations add the same products in different orders (blocked matrix kernels in PyTorch, plain loops in TypeScript), and floating-point addition is not associative, so the last bit or two can differ. A difference near 10⁻⁶ on activations of size one to ten is a few float32 steps. A real bug, such as a wrong mask entry or a missing norm, moves values by 10⁻² or more.
Run the parity test in your browser

python/parity.py exports real contexts together with every intermediate activation of the PyTorch model. The test suite then rebuilds each context with the TypeScript engine and compares the two forward passes stage by stage. The sampler, rebuilt independently

The forward-pass checks start from contexts built by the TypeScript sampler, so the sampler needs its own check. A separate Python program re-implements pre.rs, fly.rs and the masks directly from the Rust and Python sources , rebuilds thousands of contexts from the raw databases, and compares every token, the order in which rows were visited, and the masks. It uses an exact copy of the site’s random-number generator, so both programs make the same random draws.

The unit tests pin down the behavior the spec describes: preprocessing statistics on the spec’s toy database, the sampler’s invariants (one target, the seed first, parents before children, the temporal filter, the width bound, the hard stop at L), the masks of the spec’s worked example, the forward pass against PyTorch, and properties of the generated databases. The paper and the paper-era code were first distilled into a technical specification, the “spec” cited throughout this course, and the engine was written against it. Every non-trivial fact in it carries a citation: a file and line of the official code, a page of the paper, or a small script that checked it. The counts below are read from the spec’s text.

Then reviewers with three lenses (model, data, training) tried to break it. Each proposed correction was re-checked against the code, the repository’s git history, the arXiv versions of the paper and the PyTorch 2.6.0 source, and the outcome was logged in §14 . sections.title: What is scaled down, and what is different
blocks: Scale is the only thing this site changes on purpose. Every operation, from the preprocessing formulas to the decoders, follows the paper-era code. A handful of other differences come with running in a browser on a laptop. For each one, the question that matters is whether it changes the mathematics or only the rounding.
Model size
same operations
Paper
d = 256, 8 heads, 12 blocks, 22,336,131 parameters
This site
d = 64, 4 heads, 4 blocks, 535,491 parameters
The same modules with narrower tensors and fewer blocks. Both counts are computed here from the module shapes of model.py; the paper’s matches its “22.3M” .
Context size
same operations
Paper
This site

The sampler is the same algorithm at any (L, w); the cross-check below runs it at four settings, the paper’s included . Our databases are small, so a short context already reaches the seed’s neighborhood.
Data
different numbers learned
Paper
RelBench: 7 databases, pretraining on the 6 not under test
This site
4 synthetic databases, pretraining on the 3 that are not ShopDB
Same protocol, leave one database out . The learned weights and every metric are this site’s own and are never compared with the paper’s tables on one axis.
Precision
rounding only
Paper
bfloat16 weights, cell values, text embeddings and optimizer state; RMSNorm ε = 2⁻⁷
This site
float32 throughout, embeddings included; RMSNorm ε pinned to 2⁻⁷

float32 keeps 24 significant bits where bfloat16 keeps 8, so our numbers are closer to the exact maths, not further from it. The official preprocessing stores the text embeddings as raw bf16 and rounds cell values to bf16 when it builds a batch . ε is pinned so that RMSNorm divides by the same √(mean x² + ε) as in the paper environment .
Random numbers
different random draws
Paper
Rust StdRng (ChaCha12), seeded with epoch + seed row + seed
This site
xoshiro128** with the same seed formula, drawn at the same points

Wherever the sampler draws (which child row to keep, which frontier entry to expand), the two generators pick different rows, so a given context is not bit-identical to Rust’s. The distribution over contexts is the same . The audit below shows what the draws decide.
Attention kernel
rounding only
Paper
compiled FlexAttention with block masks
This site
dense masked softmax (PyTorch port); per-query loops over allowed keys (browser)

One function, three kernels: softmax over the allowed keys, scale 1/√d_head, 0 for a query with no allowed key . Only the order of floating-point additions differs; the figure below checks it on the live context.
Training budget
different numbers learned
Paper
50,001 steps × 256 contexts × 1024 tokens on 8×A100, about 2 hours
This site
4,001 steps × 32 × 128 tokens on a CPU, 19 minutes
The paper’s model sees about 800 times more tokens (1.3 × 10¹⁰ vs 1.6 × 10⁷). The optimizer, schedule shape and selection rule are the same .
Evaluation sets
different numbers learned
Paper
at most 40 batches × 32 seeds × 8 GPUs = 10,240 seed rows per split and task (set in the code; the paper does not say)
This site
71 / 74 customer-churn rows (val / test), 6 ShopDB sets in all

The official evaluation stops after 40 batches per GPU, a fixed subset of each split . Our splits are tiny and evaluated in full, so a difference of a few AUROC points between two checkpoints is within noise.
One function, three kernels

Attention is the place where the three implementations look most different. All three compute the masked softmax of the paper, softmax(Mask(QKᵀ; M)/√d_head)·V with −∞ where the mask is 0 . FlexAttention receives the boolean mask as a block mask, skips key blocks that hold no allowed pair, and treats the remaining masked scores as −∞ . The port computes all S × S scores and fills the masked ones with −∞. The browser engine keeps, for each query, the list of its allowed keys and computes the softmax and the weighted sum over that list only.
The SDPA branch (lines 39-41) is never taken: every layer receives a mask (spec §6.1).

One case needs care: a query with no allowed key. It happens in the neighbor layer for every cell whose row has no child rows in the context. A naive dense softmax divides 0 by 0 there and returns NaN. FlexAttention’s compiled kernel replaces the zero sum by 1 and outputs 0, the port zeroes such rows explicitly, and the engine skips them . The figure recomputes one sublayer of the live forward pass the dense way and compares it with the engine’s weights.
Dense softmax vs the engine’s, on the live context

Each strip has one cell per key position of the live context (gray = padding). Raw scores use the diverging scale (blue negative, red positive). Weights use the blue sequential scale relative to the row’s largest weight; a weight of exactly 0 stays blank and red marks NaN. Hover a cell to read its values. The arrows step through the query positions. This uses the global context, so it follows your simulation settings.
What the random numbers decide

The official sampler seeds Rust’s standard generator with epoch + seed row + seed . This site uses a different generator with the same seed formula, drawing at the same two points of the algorithm and with the same ranges. The spec notes that bit-exact parity with Rust is not needed: any seeded generator gives the same distribution over contexts . What does change is which rows a given draw selects. pages.title: Who builds the task table, and how can it hold labels in a zero-shot setting?

sections.title: Who builds the task table, and how can it hold labels in a zero-shot setting?
blocks: When are the task tables created? If their cells are used in the inference step, these tables need to pre-exist to feed the transformer, right? How will they pre-exist and already have data in them if this is a new table that is being created now, and how does the algorithm know how to build these tables and populate them without knowing the context, being used in a completely zero-shot new dataset?

RT never builds a task table. It is input data, prepared before RT runs by whoever poses the prediction task: in the paper, RelBench’s task code fills every row with a label computed from what already happened in the database. The one unknown label, the seed’s, is masked. “Zero-shot” means no weight updates on the new database; you still have to say what to predict, and that task’s history reaches the model through the context window.

sections.title: RT reads task tables; it never makes them
blocks: A task table is part of the input, like the database’s own tables. It exists before preprocessing starts. The paper describes it as a table that “stores the forecasting labels, together with foreign keys linking to the relevant entities (e.g., user IDs or item IDs) and a timestamp specifying the prediction horizon” , and RT attaches it to the database: “For each task, we attach a dedicated task table to the database. Only one task table is active at a time … from the model’s perspective task tables are treated as ordinary relational tables” .
In the official code the order of events is:

Download. scripts/download_relbench.py asks RelBench for every dataset and every task. A task arrives as three ready-made files, tasks/<task>/train.parquet, val.parquet and test.parquet, labels included .

Preprocess. pre.rs reads db/*.parquet and tasks/*/*.parquet in one loop and turns both into rows and cells the same way. A task file becomes a table named after the task folder, of type Train, Val or Test .
Sample and predict. The sampler takes seed rows from that table and builds a context around each one .

No step computes a label. The repository reads the labels from these files; its only hard-coded edits to task tables cast some label columns to booleans (nonzero becomes true) and drop a stray index column .

sections.title: Who fills the rows: the task definition, run over the database’s past
blocks: RelBench does. A RelBench task is a small piece of code: an entity table, a time column, a target, a window length Δ, and a make_table(db, timestamps) method. For each timestamp t, it lists the active entities and computes each one’s label from what happened in the window (t, t + Δ] . For rel-f1/driver-dnf it is a SQL query: a driver gets did_not_finish = 1 when one of their race results in the next 30 days is not a finish.

The timestamps come from two cutoffs fixed by the dataset. Training rows step back from the validation cutoff in steps of Δ until the start of the data; validation and test rows sit at their cutoffs . RelBench refuses to build a split whose window would run past the end of the recorded data (“insufficient aggregation time”).

So a task table is a summary of history. Each label describes something that has already happened and is recorded in the database. That is why a table “created now” can be full of labels: it is created from the past. Even the test labels are on disk, and RT reads them, because the evaluation compares predictions with them .
ShopDB’s customer-churn task table, filled from the orders that already happened
The same figure as in chapter 3. Every label is a count over the orders table in the window after the row’s timestamp: nothing is predicted while the table is built.

sections.title: The one label that is unknown is masked
blocks: The label the model must predict is the seed row’s own. The sampler marks exactly that cell as the target and the mask . The model then replaces its value with a learned mask vector: the value encoder is multiplied by ~masks, the mask embedding by masks . The true value never enters the forward pass; only the loss and the metrics read it.

sections.title: Then what is “zero-shot” about it?
blocks: The paper defines zero-shot relational learning as “predicting new targets on a new RDB with a new schema, without weight updates. Information about the new RDB is available only at inference time, solely through the context window” . The definition is about the weights: none of them were trained on the new database or, in the paper’s experiments, on any table of it. It does not say the task needs no definition. Someone still decides what to predict (which entity, which outcome, which horizon), and the task table is how that decision is written down .
The model is never told what the task means. Everything it gets is cells in the context:
the target cell carries its column phrase, such as “did_not_finish of driver-dnf”, embedded as text like every other column name ;
its type picks the output: a boolean target is read as a logit, a number as a z-score ;

the context brings in earlier rows of the same task table, with their labels visible. From the seed, the sampler goes up to the entity row, then down to that entity’s other task rows with timestamps at or before the seed’s . These are the in-context labels.

The paper is explicit that this is not few-shot prompting: “While task rows provide ‘in-context labels’, our setting is not few-shot as explicit subgraph-label pairs are not required” . The labels are just more cells that the attention can read.

sections.title: And if the task has no history at all?
blocks: Then there are no past labels to put in the context, and the paper’s numbers say to expect little. Removing the target entity’s own past labels (its self labels) drops mean zero-shot AUROC from 70.1 to 53.8 . On rel-trial/study-outcome, contexts contain no labels at all (0 ± 0 per context) , and RT’s zero-shot AUROC is 51.8, next to the 50.0 of random guessing . Chapter 15 shows the same collapse on this site’s model.

The code also needs some history before it can run. Validation and test splits copy their normalization statistics from the task’s training split, so a task without a training split stops preprocessing with a panic .

sections.title: Autocomplete tasks need no task table
blocks: The other task family avoids the question entirely. An autocomplete task predicts a column that already exists, such as a review’s rating. The seed is the database row itself, its cell in that column is masked, and the in-context labels are the same column’s values in other rows that the sampler reaches. No task-table row ever enters such a context . See chapter 3 for both families on ShopDB.
